speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: RADIOACTIVE FALL-OUT
speechtext:
1.	On how many occasions has there been radioactive precipitation or fall-out in Canada following experimental tests of atomic or hydrogen bombs or weapons by the United States or by any other country?
2.	What are the dates of such radioactive precipitation or fall-out and where in Canada did the same occur?
3.	What was the extent of such radioactive precipitation or fall-out in Canada on each such occasion?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: RADIOACTIVE FALL-OUT
speechtext:
1,	2 and 3. The level of radioactivity is of interest to the Department of National Health and Welfare which has access to all data available to the Department of National Defence on this subject.
The defence research board does not systematically, or as a matter of routine, measure the extent to which radioactive debris, resulting from nuclear explosions, falls on the surface of the earth in Canada. The defence research board does measure, at various points in Canada, the radioactive content of precipitation in the form of rain or snow. While these measurements are made on a continual basis, they can only be made when rain or snow occurs. Complete data on the extent of radioactive fall-out in Canada cannot be obtained by this method.
Furthermore, the clouds of radioactive debris, which ascend rapidly into the upper reaches of the earth's atmosphere after nuclear explosions, drift around the earth, intermingling, and fall-out may continue in an irregular pattern for many months. Thus it is difficult during a test series to relate fallout on a particular day at a particular point to a specific explosion. Moreover, rain or snow is radioactive when it reaches the surface of the earth because of the natural radioactive particles always present in the atmosphere, although this natural radioactivity disappears fairly rapidly.
The important fact is not the occasion on which radioactivity has been noted at a particular location, but the total accumulated level of radioactivity resulting from all causes, including nuclear explosions. Defence research board data are incomplete on this
point but have recently been supplemented by information obtained from the U.S. atomic energy commission. At the request of the U.S. weather bureau, and on behalf of the U.S. atomic energy commission, certain Department of Transport weather stations have been making daily collections of fallout in Canada during the past year.
These collections have been measured by the U.S. atomic energy commission and, as a result, it has been determined that the highest measurement of accumulated radioactivity in the heavily populated zone of Canada, resulting from all nuclear tests carried out anywhere during 1954 was 80 millicuries per square mile on January 1, 1955. This corresponds roughly to a gamma dose rate of 3/10,000,000 of a roentgen per hour. Natural radiation corresponds to about 1/100,000 of a roentgen per hour and industrial workers are permitted to receive, if necessary, a constant dose of about 2/1,000 of a roentgen per hour.
As an example of specific fall-out at a location in eastern Canada, during the middle of March a measurement of 1,000 millicuries per square mile was made on the day of fall-out. Other studies have shown that the amount of fall-out which accumulates over a period of time is much the same in all the populated parts of Canada, the maximum being somewhat less than twice the minimum. In other words, the variation from point to point is not significant. This fall-out decays rapidly and the amount of radioactivity measured on the day previously mentioned will be only 5 millicuries per square mile on January 1, 1956.

Mr. Chairman, all our thinking
about defence today must be profoundly affected, I am sure all will agree, by recent developments in the field of atomic and thermonuclear weapons as well as in the range and speed of modern jet bombers.
I am sure that all members will agree that this applies not only in the military fields of strategy and tactics but also in the wider fields of the defence of our civilian population and of the preservation of our industrial potential.
These new developments also give to our foreign policy a greater importance and a greater sense of urgency than ever before.
There is today no absolute defence against atomic and thermonuclear weapons in the quantities in which they could be aggressively brought to bear on this or any other country. That does not mean that we may not blunt and minimize such an attack. That does not mean that we could not survive such an attack. The powers of resistance and the ingenuity of human beings are very great indeed, as we saw in the last world war.
We may lessen the effectiveness of such an attack by such powers and measures as we can contrive, but we cannot wholly prevent damage to a country geographically as large as Canada. In other words, there is no 100 per cent perfect defence which will prevent such an attack from meeting with some degree of success if it is made.
It follows, therefore, that since Canada, by herself, can provide only a limited though substantial amount of defence, and since other free countries are in the same position, greater assurance against the risks of war can be attained only by collective security. That is, of course, the meaning of NATO-of fifteen nations working to one end-a great joint defence effort on the part of all for the protection of each.
I should like to say at this point that Canadians, generally, welcome the German people as our full and equal partners in NATO. The accession of the Federal Republic of Germany is important, not only because it will eventually strengthen the defence forces of the free world, but also because time may well prove that this enlargement of NATO is in itself a significant milestone along the path to the ultimate brotherhood of nations and the abolition of war.
Within this NATO team, Canada has the role of providing some measures of defence at home and some abroad. It is to this end that we are providing sea, land and air forces. But we do not, and we cannot, provide
Supply-National Defence weapons and forces of all types and in the numbers which might be required for the complete defence of all Canada in a global war, if that should come. It would be quite beyond the resources, both physical and financial, of a country embracing such a vast area as ours does, and relatively so sparsely populated, to carry out such a tremendous undertaking by itself.
One of the great advantages of the NATO alliance is that it permits each of its members to specialize in the roles for which it is best fitted, and, while providing such specialized help to other members of the team, to rely likewise on assistance from them in other fields of defence in which they are most proficient.
And it is folly in any event for us, or for a potential enemy, or for anyone, to talk today about "winning" a war. The tremendous powers of death, destruction and contamination of thermonuclear warfare today simply beggar description.
Our hope under such circumstances would simply be not to lose the war, rather than to expect to win it. And in this case there is a vast difference between "not losing" and "winning".
That is why the central concept of Canada's defence policy today is the maintenance of peace-peace assured by such overwhelming collective strength that no potential aggressor will dare to put the issue to the test.
We must seek increasingly, by every means within our power and in conjunction with our friends, to prevent the outbreak of a major war, which, if it came, could only bring chaos and catastrophe for everyone involved.
Together with our allies we must make it abundantly clear that violent aggression will be answered instantaneously by all-out retaliation throughout the homeland of the aggressor. And we must show as well our determination and our capacity to survive a sudden attempt at a knock-out blow and to fight our way back to stability and freedom as quickly as we can.
That is why we have the 1st Canadian air division in Europe with twelve squadrons of first-class fighter planes.
That is why we have the 1st Canadian infantry brigade there to help defend freedom in Europe.
That is why we have fighting ships and planes ready to patrol the North Atlantic sea-lanes against the submarine menace.
That is why we have here in Canada a mobile striking force of three airborne battalions ready to meet possible local attacks instantaneously.

Supply-National Defence That is why, working with the United States, we are extending a complex radar warning network across this land's vast distances, and out into the neighbouring oceans.
That is why, in the North American air spaces, Canadian and United States interceptor planes, aided by radar and ground observers, are constantly watching and checking unidentified aircraft.
And that is why, since NATO was formed six years ago, Canada has contributed military aid to our European friends to a value substantially in excess of one billion dollars, and is training year by year approximately 1,000 air crew for our allies.
All of these vital elements of our defence effort here and in Europe are to help make the nations of the north Atlantic community capable of checking an aggressor and of striking back so vigorously as to destroy his war potential.
The balance between our forces in Canada and our forces beyond our borders is based on the sound judgment of our military advisers as to where, in present circumstances, Canadian fighting men can best maintain our freedom and that of the free world.
While no special arrangements exist for provision of forces to meet commitments which may be made from time to time in support of the activities of the United Nations, we have, I think, demonstrated in the support given in the Korean war that we can, when the necessity arises, carry out our proper part promptly and effectively.
The great field of the United Nations, generally speaking, lies, of course, in the realm of negotiations, the development of understanding and the peaceful solution of difficulties, rather than in the provision of armed forces.
I said a few minutes ago that the central concept of Canada's defence policy was the maintenance of peace, and I said further that the best hope of maintaining peace lay in the maintenance by the free nations of overwhelming strength.
I am concerned, of course, with the military aspects of this strength, but there are, of course, other important ways in which we may make sincere efforts toward establishing permanent peace. Whatever we are able to do through the exchange of ideas, the development of understanding, the extension of friendly trade relations, the assistance rendered to underdeveloped lands, will cumulatively prove perhaps more important than we sometimes realize.

This policy of employing civilians in support of the armed forces is one which is followed by most modern nations because it is a policy which results in substantial economies of time and money.
The average civilian salary today within the department is approximately $2,600 a year. The pay and allowances of an average uniformed man is of the order of $3,600 a year, or, if the cost of travel is included, about $4,000 a year.
I think it is obvious that it is very much in the public interest that civilians be employed, wherever possible, and subject to a limitation which I shall mention in a moment. As a matter of fact, our ratio is about 1 civilian to 2-1 uniformed personnel. This ratio follows closely the experience of the United Kingdom and of the United States. In the United Kingdom the ratio is exactly the same as ours. In the United States the ratio is slightly lower-1 civilian to 2-9 uniformed personnel. Unless our ratio is to change substantially, it is obvious, I think, that the number of civilian personnel will grow proportionately as the numbers of the armed services increase.
The limitation which I just mentioned regarding the rule of employing civilians to support the armed forces is this-the armed forces are organized to fight, if necessary, outside the territorial boundaries of Canada. In order to fight under active service conditions, supporting personnel-logistic, medical, etc.,-must be immediately available and they must be military personnel. This means that there must always be in peacetime a uniformed nucleus of the required supporting organizations ready to proceed into action.
Our aim is to keep a proper balance between military and civilian personnel within the department on the basis of the work being performed.
Perhaps hon. members would be interested if I were to refer briefly to the way we check the creation of civilian positions. To ensure that ample care is taken and the creation of civilian positions is checked, we have service complement committees which review periodically every position, existing or proposed, both military and civilian, and screen every application for additional staff as well. Membership on the service complement committee is an exacting and full-time job. As an added check the findings of the complement committees are further screened by the civil service commission and treasury board staff before approval of any new position is authorized.
I should like now to say a special word about the defence of the Canada-United States region-generally referred to as continental defence.


For nearly a century and a half, there has been no fighting of any consequence on Canadian territory; but we can no longer count on being an ocean away from war. Working closely with the United States we must now be ready to reckon with attacks right here on our own continent.
To meet this threat a closely integrated system of air defence, comprising early warning chains, a network of communications and intercepting forces, air and ground, has been evolved in full agreement with our neighbours to the south and is now being built up.
This is a huge, difficult and expensive task for the defence of both countries. As an example of the costs involved, I might say that the present estimated cost of the mid-Canada line, which will be wholly borne by this country, is approximately $170 million.
With this estimate for the mid-Canada line, and it is still only an estimate, and Canada's share of the cost of the "Pinetree" system, which will be approximately $151 million, it is seen that this country is contributing on these two counts alone nearly one-third of a billion dollars to the joint Canada-United States warning and control system.
In this task of continental defence there are those who urge that Canada should be wholly responsible for all defence installations on Canadian soil, and there are also those who argue that since these installations are largely for the benefit of the United States, that country should find the men and money to make them possible.
I should think that the right balance probably lies somewhere between these extreme positions. It is difficult to foresee the future nature and extent of these joint defences, but up to the present we have succeeded in finding a mutually agreeable basis for sharing responsibility in these projects as they arise.
I am confident, as in the past, the friendly co-operation between our two countries will continue to be an example to the free world -an example of great concern to the free world because in addition to our own immediate defence we must never forget that the safeguarding of the strategic air forces of the United States and the industrial potential of both countries is of vital importance to every member of NATO.
I feel that in our thinking about defence matters today, the crying need is for realism. Let us not fool ourselves: absolute security cannot be purchased, and any reasonable measure of security comes high. And Canada's defence program must be kept within some sensible money limits if we are to be able, year after year, to sustain it.
By further streamlining our administrative practices, we can also effect some economies,

but it is, let me assure you, quite illusory to think that very substantial cuts can be made in our defence estimates without weakening our defence effort.
We hear, almost daily, suggestions that Canada should undertake increased defence activities of numerous sorts, many of them, no doubt, desirable, if we could afford them. We rarely hear it argued, however, that we should spend more on defence than we are spending today.
In peace, and in our common pursuit of the abundance that science and human ingenuity and hard work can provide for the great masses of humanity, no thinking person wants to see war delay or turn aside mankind's long and patient pilgrimage towards a better life.
While our hearts cherish the hope of a world without war, in these uneasy years our defence preparations give the best substance to this hope.
The present climate of international affairs appears to be moderating, but we cannot be sure that the better weather of recent months will endure. Our objective remains fixed before us-to make peace permanent. With this in mind, the free nations are willing to negotiate with the U.S.S.R.-at the summit, at any level-but we must negotiate from strength.
Defence is costly and will no doubt continue so. But standing resolutely and together with the other free peoples, Canadians are willing to pay dearly to maintain their way of life.
To do this, we must go on so far as we can see, year after year, investing a substantial part of our national production in defence.
After all, the reward for our defence preparedness is immeasurable: for what we do to guard against the possibility of war is our best guarantee that our time will be a time of peace.

In commencing a review of these estimates for national defence, Mr. Chairman, I would call attention to the fact that once again the appropriation for this department is the largest single appropriation in the whole of the estimates for the carrying on of the essential services of this country. There is some $1,775 million allocated for the Department of National Defence, to which must be added some $200 million which is the special credit accounts. We are asked, therefore, for some $65 million more than was actually expended last year. With the credits, as I have said, of some $200 million the estimates for this department amount in total to $1,975 million, to which
Supply-National Defence must be added the estimates in kindred departments such as the Department of Defence Production of somewhere in the neighbourhood of $23 million and civil defence of some $7 million. This makes a grand total for national defence and its kindred departments of over $2 billion.
We do not criticize the amount of money which is being allocated for what the minister has described this morning as the preservation of peace. This party never has criticized the amount of money which the government, over the past ten years, has been asking for that purpose. We are just as anxious as those who sit on the other side of the house for the preservation of peace and to make peace permanent.
Before I start offering some comments on the policy which is being adopted for the expenditure of these vast sums of money, I should like to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Campney) on assuming the appointment of Minister of National Defence. The present minister took over this portfolio on July 1 last year. Though we may from time to time differ on questions of policy, and particularly matters of detail, I can assure him that we all wish him well in his extremely difficult task.
I do want to say one word about his predecessor. Canada has been fortunate in the years gone by in that whenever there has been a national crisis we have found a man with the capacity to fill the important position of national defence. When the Hon. Brooke Claxton took over that responsibility there was a national crisis before this country. War seemed imminent, and war did break out in Korea very shortly. The defences of Canada were at a low ebb. They had been reduced to that low ebb by a policy of rather hasty demobilization after world war II. It was no light task which confronted the Hon. Brooke Claxton, and in that critical situation he was able to build up Canada's forces to meet that immediate situation and to lay plans for a three or five year defence program which, in large measure, has been fulfilled and which certainly met the needs of the intervening years. I think that the Hon. Brooke Claxton, although there were many times when I felt it was desirable to criticize his policy and the details of the way in which that policy was carried out, will go down in history with his name parallel with the names of other great Canadian ministers of national defence.
His passing from the house to take over a civilian position really brings to a close an era. He met the immediate situation which confronted the country at the time. He devised

Supply-National Defence a pattern of our defence forces which was designed to meet similar emergencies.
As I said, that program is nearly completed; that era is finished. The new minister starts off with a clean slate. He starts off to meet new and very difficult problems which face the country today. I say that an era has been completed, because there has been no event of greater importance during the last 12 months than the emergence of the thermonuclear bomb, and the knowledge we possess that other countries also have developed that bomb.
Therefore the new minister is posed with a set of entirely new problems the solution of which will require a great deal of courage. Such problems were reflected in the speech he made this morning, when he placed increasing emphasis on the part we must play in the continental defence of the North American continent, in the hope that world peace may be preserved. He emphasized the sentiments which were expressed by Sir Winston Churchill at Westminster not so long ago, when he expressed the hope that the emergence of the H-bomb would contribute more to world peace than to world war. We sincerely hope that that will prove to be the case. But we are not in a position at the present time to be lulled into any false sense of security, any more than we should be paralysed by fear that no absolute protection can be found against this terrible weapon.
In the white paper, to which the minister has referred, he mentioned on several occasions the appalling destructive power of these new thermonuclear weapons. At page 3 of the white paper, following the contents page, he refers to the fact that in addition to certain changes which had already been mentioned-
-appraisals of new weapons, new tactical and strategic concepts, and demands for increased mobility and flexibility of forces make it evident that changes in emphasis must be made from time to time within the defence programs of the NATO member nations.
Then he goes on to say:
Canada will continue to make such adjustments in her defence program. Current developments in the build-up of air defences on this continent, which are changes of emphasis of this order, enable Canada to make a highly important contribution to NATO as a whole.
And later on he says:
In co-operation with the United States we are providing additional warning networks and increasingly effective and co-ordinated air defence forces on this continent. By so doing we are of course meeting a common need for home defence and, beyond that, we are also assisting in the protection of the industrial potential of North America.
He has reiterated those principles during his remarks today. We concur in them. We


believe that Canada is making a contribution to NATO by taking part in the joint defence of this North American continent. We believe we must share in that team play- and it must be team play-for the development of the defence of this continent. We are not a country which can provide all the defences required. We are in partnership with the United States of America in providing defences here. But we do want to play our fair share in that team; we do not want to be considered as a very indifferent player. We feel we have as important a role in the defence and the protection of this North American continent as has any other country; and we cherish certain sovereign rights which we feel are ours, although we recognize as a fact that to a certain extent sovereignty must be surrendered in order to play our part in the continental defence of the country, and to expect the other country that is vitally interested in the defence of this North American continent to provide her part.
Those are the sentiments which were running through the minister's speech this morning, and they are certainly the principles and the opinions expressed in the first two pages of the white paper. As I say, in the main, we concur in those principles. But when one comes to look through the other pages of this white paper, one is appalled by their emptiness and by the barren attempts to implement the policies which have been described in the first two pages.
Canada's position is unique. Canada lies across approaches-and the approaches are only by air and by sea-to the great industrial centres of this North American continent. The minister said, in effect that it was more important that we should not lose the war rather than to win it, and that perhaps more emphasis should be placed upon not losing the war than upon winning it. The only place where a war against democracy could be lost is on this North American continent; and Canada is in the position where she must play her part in guarding the approaches to that one vital area.
The threat of course is that of an attack coming by air over the roof of the world, using the approaches from Europe across the Arctic and down through the eastern portions of Canada to the great industrial centres of eastern United States, and also that of using similar approaches in the west from Siberia to the great industrial centres of western Canada and western United States on the Pacific seaboard.
The only major threat which can come is an airborne threat. It is fantastic to think that large armies could be landed on the Arctic shores of Canada and advanced

through the barren lands of the great north, even though in the future those areas may carry a much greater population than they do today. The approach is by airborne troops, with a minor approach on the sea lanes leading to the east and west where perhaps some minor diversion might be carried out by submarines. But we have to be realistic, as the minister says.
The first thing that we must realize is that Canada's great role in the preservation of peace is guarding those air approaches to the only places where the war could be lost. The threat of airborne forces will be mainly directed against the centres of industry. It will very largely be an airborne bombing attack, but it is possible that attempts may be made to seize certain airfields in the north, or to hold for a period or to destroy certain vital centres such as important mining areas where vital minerals are being produced.
To meet that airborne attack we must have strong air forces to cope with the air forces of any potential enemy. We must realize the fact that Canada cannot produce by herself all these air forces. We must rely to a certain extent on the air forces of the United States because the United States are playing on this team with us. In the general plans it is not Canada's role to spend money-and I do not think we have the money to spend- on any fleet of strategic bombers; therefore, let us concentrate on the protection of those air approaches.
Oh, a good many statements have been made recently and in the past couple of years on the fact that greater emphasis is being placed on the air arm of Canada. It is well for us to take a look and see how much greater emphasis has been placed on the air arm of Canada. I looked at the distribution of the defence dollar in 1951-52 when this program was first brought into effect. In that year the proportion of the defence dollar allocated to the R.C.A.F. for air defence was 46.6 per cent. Today, after two years during which we have been told that greater emphasis is being placed on the air arm of Canada, the amount of the defence dollar devoted to the air force is 42.2 per cent. Is there any increasing emphasis being placed on defence in the air? Are we trying to fool ourselves and to believe that just because more men have been taken into the air force than there were previously there has been any considerable reorientation between the various services? Are we really being realistic? May I ask the minister, Mr. Chairman, is he really being realistic when he reduces the percentage of the defence dollar placed in the air from 46.6 per cent in 1951-52 to 42.2 per cent this year?

On the actual amount spent; thank you. But in the actual amount allocated for last year and the actual amount allocated for this year-we trust that the amount allocated this year will be spent during the year-there is a reduction of $109 million,
I regret to say.
Regarding the strength of the air force, we have in the air defence command nine squadrons of regular R.C.A.F. squadrons for the defence of Canada, which are to be equipped by the end of this year with CF-100's. Today I believe there are only some three of those squadrons actually equipped.
Reference was made to the ten auxiliary squadrons. I am pleased that the minister acknowledged the difficulties. It was the first acknowledgment that has been made in this house, although I and others have pointed out the difficulties there would be in getting personnel of the auxiliary squadrons trained so that they could take part in the role which they were now called upon to fulfil, namely, manning modern aircraft for the defence of Canada to be ready at a moment's notice.
Last year and the year before I remember stressing the necessity of very considerably increasing the number of regular personnel who were attached to and carried on training with the auxiliary squadrons. If the auxiliary squadrons are to be the backbone of the defence of Canada, then we must have a very large number of permanent personnel attached to them. I do not believe it is practical for the auxiliary squadrons to carry out the role assigned to them. I think we had better be realistic. I think we had better say that we have to carry these ten auxiliary squadrons as regular squadrons in addition to the nine squadrons that we have.
We are told in the white paper that the 41 squadrons which were called for in the program are now being organized, and reference is made to the fact that they are being maintained. I am not at all clear as to what is meant by the words "being

Supply-National Defence organized" and "being maintained". They can be organized on paper and they can be maintained by skeleton crews. Are we to understand from the statement in the white paper that personnel ready to man these various squadrons are now available, in being and in uniform and that they have been allocated to the various duties which they would have to perform if they were going to operate these various squadrons? I think that that point must be cleared up because on it hinges a great deal regarding our manpower problem.
I would call attention to the fact that we feel-I feel anyway-that the greatest danger to this continent lies in the northern approaches by air and that we must meet that air threat with airborne troops. We only have four transport squadrons of the R.C.A.F. to carry out the tasks connected with the north in supplying not only the R.C.A.F. but any army troops that might be in the north, as well as to carry out necessary supply duties in Europe.
I feel that we have to be realistic again. The number of transport squadrons must be increased if we are to carry out those duties. A heavy burden will fall upon the transport squadrons of the R.C.A.F. when the mid-Canada and the D.E.W. lines are established and maintained. I have no doubt that they are now being used to carry out some of the construction work but permanent maintenance work will be required. If we have not the transport squadrons to do it then another country will have to supply them.
The minister referred to the army and outlined the army establishments. As an old soldier I was delighted to hear that he did not agree with the statements which have been made by his own department about scrapping the army. That is not a thought that has ever entered my head. No, the army should not be scrapped but the army must adjust its organizations to its principal role.
I do not believe in maintaining yesterday's establishments in order to fight the war of tomorrow. There is a danger that we keep to time-honoured traditions and formations which have now become time-worn. I have made similar expressions over the years. I was looking over some of my previous remarks which I had intended to read, but I do not think it is necessary for me to do so. In the debates of 1946, 1948 and 1949 I stressed the need for taking a new look at the army organization and organizing our army for the needs which confront it or for the role which it has to fill in the future.
We are told that the army consists of the 1st Canadian division, consisting of the 1st, 

2nd and 3rd infantry brigades, supporting arms and auxiliary troops, and a fourth brigade in addition to those three brigades. The order of battle of that division is very similar to the order of battle of a division which took part in the fighting on the Somme in 1915 or in the early part of world war II in 1940 and 1941. There is very little change in the proportions of infantry, artillery, engineers, army service corps and so forth. I wonder whether our organization has not been based more on tradition than on the needs of today.
We have a brigade in Germany which no doubt is carrying out the wishes of the NATO commanders that there should be an infantry brigade in Germany equipped with the most modern weapons to let the people of western Europe know that Canadian soldiers will if necessary be fighting in West Germany. That was all right four or five years ago and it is necessary for us to keep up replacements for that brigade, but does it fit into the new picture? When the divisions of West Germany are fully organized and equipped it is questionable whether we shall be required to keep one brigade there.
Even supposing one brigade is kept there we have three other brigades as well as a mobile striking force of the three battalions the minister mentioned in his speech here in Canada, plus all the divisional troops.
I do not believe that that is the kind of army which fits into our role of defending the air approaches to the North American continent.
I cannot believe that we shall be sending divisions of infantry, divisional artillery, divisional engineers and divisional army service corps into the north country to deal with the type of attack to which I have referred, that is airborne attacks with the idea of seizing some point of strategic importance.
The emphasis over and over again is that the principal role for Canada to play in this team for the preservation of world peace is to organize our army so that it can play that role. I think our whole army in Canada should be a straight airborne army, that our forces should not be built up on the establishments which were so valuable in world war I and world war II. They should be designed so that they can be rapidly moved from their home stations to deal with the problem of recapturing or defending some area which might be attacked.
Let us remember that if an attempt is made by an enemy, for instance, to seize northern airfields, the use of bombs by the R.C.A.F. and the United States air force will be more effective than an attempt to move mechanized artillery up there to support any

counter-attack. I am firmly of the opinion that if we are to keep any army there are certain things we must do. I believe we should keep it. I do not subscribe to the idea of scrapping the army but I believe you will find that the army will be scrapped if it is not brought up to modern conditions. I believe it will die because the average young Canadian, who is an intelligent man, will realize that he is being asked to serve in an army which was effective years ago but which is not designed with any realistic interpretation of the role it has to carry out today.
As to this talk of lowering the morale of the army because there is criticism of it, may I say that I do not believe a word of it. I believe that you will raise the morale of the army and that you will bring recruits into the army if you make it clear that it has a modern role to fulfil and not a role which is time-worn. There must be an entirely new concept of our army formation. In the British white paper reference was made to the army being organized along the lines of fire brigades. That is the sort of thing we want, namely fire brigade formations. I do not mean fire brigades to extinguish fire and I do not wish to equip them with fire engines, but I mean fire brigade formations ready and available at a moment's notice, as soon as the warning goes out, to concentrate from various areas with highly mobile airborne forces in order to destroy any enemy that may have landed from the air.
I was pleased to see that the minister is perhaps thinking along those lines when he stressed that our army was mainly an infantry army. I think it is becoming more and more an infantry army equipped with the latest possible weapons. I cannot see our army being employed in Canada on any large divisional formation basis. So much tor the army.
I turn now to the navy role to which the minister referred. He again, as was his predecessor year after year, was optimistic as to when the destroyer escorts would be available. In the white paper of 1951-52, published on June 30, 1951, we were told that the keels of four escort vessels had been laid, two in Montreal and one at each coast. The white paper goes on to say that these four vessels are expected to be launched in 1951 or early in 1952.
I am encouraged to hear the minister say that he hopes that by the end of this year they will be commissioned. I hope so too. I realize the difficulties which have confronted this shipbuilding program. I should like to refer to the Minister of Defence Production and tell him to use some of these powers that he has had for so long-
Supply-National Defence Mr. Howe (Port Arthur): That is why I need them.

-to produce these vessels. However that may be, I realize that changes come about, and that alterations brought about by the changing role of the navy have caused delays in connection with the commissioning of these vessels.
I feel that there is a changing role. In 1951 I think our principal role was that of convoy escort and an anti-submarine role.
I do not place the same emphasis on the convoy role as I did in those days or as the government did. I cannot see the likelihood of large forces of Canadian troops or United States troops having to be convoyed during war across the ocean. But I do think that there is an important role, as far as antisubmarine work is concerned, in guarding our shores. We have sea approaches as well as air approaches to this continent. Modern submarines can come within a reasonable distance and from those submarines can be launched missiles or even aircraft which could carry some of these thermonuclear bombs. But encouraging experiments have been carried out elsewhere with atomic depth charges and perhaps the submarine menace may not be as great in the future as it has been in the past because these atomic depth charges may make it extremely difficult for a hostile submarine to come within our area. In trying to locate a target, the degree of accuracy required in the use of an atomic depth charge would not be nearly as great as that required in the use of an ordinary depth charge. I therefore feel that there is perhaps a new role appearing for the navy. I urge the importance of flexibility in that service and of making the fullest possible use of reconnaissance planes and helicopters working with the fleet air arm. Possibly the greatest danger we may have to face will be the mine of the future, and our efforts must be concentrated on meeting that danger.
So much for the general outlook and the sort of policy that I think should be followed in order to preserve the peace of the future. I believe we must face up to the problem now. I believe the minister must take into consideration now what the future pattern will be. I said he was starting with a clean slate and that we are starting on a new era. I believe we are starting on a new era in which there will be uncertain peace rather than cold war and the fear of outbreaks^ of small wars all over the world. It is going to be a long time before the final day of peace comes. We must now pattern our forces on a long-term basis. The problems which faced the minister's predecessor-those of having to meet the immediate future and

Supply-National Defence to meet an emergency at once-have now passed. I referred to the army. We must give consideration to the size of the army for the reason if for no other reason than that we must consider the construction and housing problem.
In the white paper the minister referred to the permanent home stations. I notice that over the years some $800 million has been spent on construction, mainly for the provision of barracks and married quarters. According to the figures given in the white paper there are today something like 27,000 married quarters constructed, under construction or immediately planned. Are we going to keep up in peacetime this army of one division, plus one brigade, plus the striking force of three battalions, plus all the additional troops as well? Are we going to build permanent quarters for a force of that size? The amount of $161 million is allocated for construction this year. I believe it is imperative that we should provide proper barracks and accommodation for our regular troops but we cannot afford to build more accommodation than is required-not accommodation required for today but accommodation required for the future.
tha.t the Korean affair is over, now that there is a lessening of tension in Europe as the minister says, now that our attention has to be directed to the defence of this continent, I think we have got to re-examine our construction program. Reference is made to permanent stations at Chilliwack, Calgary Edmonton, Rivers, Shilo, Winnipeg, Borden Petawawa, Barriefield, Gagetown and many other places. Do we need all these? We do if we are going to maintain the kind of army outlmed in the white paper. From the manpower aspect I wonder whether we can maintain the army at its present strength. I have already raised the question whether the manpower requirements of the air force are actually being met. I am pleased to see that there has been a slight increase in the number of men m the R.C.A.F. since the 31st of December and that all the figures are reaching the ceilings that have been indicated. But I want to have the assurance that the ceilings, particularly as far as the air force is concerned, are realistic and that they provide the personnel to man the squadrons indicated in the blue book. I want to know whether "now organized and being maintained" means that these squadrons are actually in being with the personnel there and that the ceiling of 51,000 will actually meet the requirements at all times. I want to be assured that if there are not enough personnel to take over the ten 

auxiliary squadrons of the R.C.A.F. there are at least sufficient numbers to give them enough personnel to make these squadrons effective.
There is reason for some concern. I am not relying merely on rumours and statements that have been made outside the house, but we have been told that it has become necessary for United States personnel to man some stations on the "Pinetree" line, that they will be supplying the personnel to man in part, if not wholly, the D.E.W. line and the mid-Canada line. In the past I have emphasized the necessity of designing our forces to meet the needs of the defence of the country. I do not believe it would have been necessary for us to have imported 3,000 Americans to man these lines if we had trained soldiers for those particular duties instead of training them for a European campaign. I do not care whether these radar stations are manned by men wearing blue or khaki uniforms. It does not make any difference. You will find that there is going to be a much closer merging of the army and the air force than there has ever been before, and it may be that in the future they will wear the same uniform. A soldier can man a radar station just as well as an airman, and it is immaterial as long as the work is being done.
When it comes to the question of manning our own warning system I think that the principal responsibility should rest on Canadian rather than American forces. Yes, the growing need so far as this matter is concerned is to be realistic. Have we got enough men in sight to provide an effective air force, an effective army and an effective navy as designed in the white paper? We have heard statements made by various organizations pointing out the difficulty of raising the necessary men. The Canadian Legion has urged a form of national service in order to meet the needs. I have not heard the government declare its position regarding the desirability or otherwise of national service or a form of conscription. I do not believe it is necessary at the present time if proper application of the manpower available is made.
But we have got to face the fact that in order to raise the 117,000 men now in the regular forces the sum of $5,854,580 has been spent on recruiting during the past twelve months. That is a pretty large amount of money to be spent for that purpose.
I should like to say a word regarding the question of civil defence which was raised by the minister. I realize that the civil defence appropriations are not administered by his department, but civil defence is closely linked with the whole defence of the continent and, as it has already been referred

to, I trust, Mr. Chairman, that you will allow me to make a few observations regarding the matter at this time. I think that the armed forces must play an increasing role in civil defence and that you cannot divorce civil defence entirely from the rest of the defence of the country. I believe that part of the training of all regular personnel, and of all reserve and auxiliary personnel, should be in civil defence duties as well as military training. It should not necessarily take second place in their training. Due importance should be attached to the training of regular personnel in civil defence duties. After all, a lot of these men will be taking their discharges and then they will go into civilian life. If they have had a thorough training in elementary civil defence problems, they will be a valuable contribution to the civil defence organizations of this country.
Of course, many of the duties in which men in the forces are trained will be invaluable. One only needs to think of the valuable assistance that signallers would give, that engineers would give or that the army service corps units could supply to civil defence. The one thing about which I am surprised is that when our militia was being reorganized more emphasis was not placed upon retaining those units as a mobile civil defence corps. Last year when I was speaking on the civil defence estimates, I called attention to the fact that mobile corps were being established for civil defence in the United Kingdom. I believe that not only could many men have been retained in those units which were scattered throughout the country, which in many cases were disbanded or amalgamated with others, if they could have been allocated to civil defence duties, but a greater use could have been made of the training which these men had had in the past. By the very fact that in such localities there was an organization of disciplined men, even though they had been trained as gunners, infantrymen or in any other branch of the service, if they had been changed over to a militia corps for mobile civil defence, I believe it would have kept that organization alive and vital in these areas and they would have been of better service than breaking them up or disbanding them.
I think that in the future greater emphasis should be placed by the militia of today, as it is now called, or the reserve army of a year ago, in civil defence duties. I would go so far as to say that the prime role of the militia in the future should be civil defence. I do not know whether the minister will agree with that. I realize that certain of the
Supply-National Defence reserve army units may have to be earmarked to meet a strategic reserve or something of that nature, but in the majority of the reserve army or militia units I believe the primary role should be civil defence duties. I feel they should be worked into civil defence organizations. Their equipment should be allocated to them with that object in mind, and this would give some reality to the reserve army or militia training. Of course, I believe that these remarks apply not only to the army but also to the auxiliary forces in the air force and the navy. All men in the services from now on should receive civil defence training. We have got to raise the importance of civil defence. It must be realized that it is very definitely a part of our whole defence program.
Now, Mr. Chairman, that brings me to the end of my remarks on the general policy of this department. When we begin to deal with the various items there will be questions we shall require to ask. I have no doubt you intend to follow the procedure that has been followed in recent years of calling the various items as given in the details in the back of the blue book. This will enable us to have an orderly debate and an orderly question period. That, I believe the minister will agree, will save time.
I finish up where I started by again wishing the minister success in his great responsibilities. I hope he will, as a previous minister in another department used to say, take my remarks in a kindly fashion because they are intended to be constructive rather than critical. I believe we have got to work as a nation in order to carry out the very important role that we have. If I differ in some respects from the policy which he has outlined, I do so sincerely because I believe that he has a great opportunity and he has great responsibilities in a period of time when we face an entirely new set of conditions as a result of the introduction of these thermonuclear bombs. This has resulted in a greatly increased emphasis on the defence of the approaches to this continent. He starts with a clean slate, and I wish him well in fulfilling his important role.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was very pleased this morning to hear the minister placing emphasis on collective security and on peace. He was followed by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, who pretty well

Supply-National Defence placed his faith in the same moral and physical features of our defence. I do hope the minister will continue to lay stress on peace as the only possible solution to the troubles of the modern world. I am satisfied that no other way can be found to have real and permanent happiness and security, except through our efforts on behalf of world peace.
Taking part in this debate, I realize the handicap that is common to all hon. members, namely the lack of information, intimate information particularly, about Canada's defence program. Therefore I must depend largely upon what information can be gleaned from the press, and some from the white paper-although I think they should have carried the theme right through and made it perfectly white, leaving the printing off. Had they done so, we would have had just as much information.
The estimates now before the committee are to my mind the most important that will be placed before us at this session. The cost of Canada's defence is almost 50 per cent of our total budget. It is the duty of members to see that such a vast sum of money is spent in an economical and practical way for the defence of Canada.
Some of us have wondered if we are getting value for our money. Others have wondered if Canada has a defence system worthy of the name. This group is prepared to support any realistic and practical program for the defence of Canada; but we shall take issue with the government if they continue the present policy of manufacturing, and training troops with, obsolete weapons. The need for defence is possibly as great today as at any time in our history. Indeed the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) indicated the other day that the situation is worse than it was three years ago.
The most singular and startling development since the defence estimates were voted here a year ago has been what all the experts call a technological break-through in the development of nuclear weapons. In the past two years, and more particularly in the last year, warfare has been completely revolutionized as a result of the sweeping technological changes in battlefield weapons. These weapons no longer exist merely in the minds of planners, nor are they still on the drawing boards. Many of them are in actual production, and some have already been used to equip American, British and Soviet armed forces.
Military experts indicate, as the minister and the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich indicated this morning, that with these weapons has changed the whole strategy of warfare. We are dubious if there are any trained


Canadian troops who could take part in warfare where these modern weapons would be used. There is no question that these weapons will be used in the event of another war.
The NATO council has already agreed that further military strategy is to be based on the assumption that atomic weapons will be employed tactically in the event of Russian aggression. Field Marshal Montgomery, deputy supreme allied commander in Europe, has declared:
I want to make it absolutely clear that we at supreme headquarters are basing all our operational planning on using atomic and thermonuclear weapons in our defence. With us it is no longer "They may possibly be used". It is very definitely "They will be used", if we are attacked.
The United States also has been outspoken regarding the use of thermonuclear weapons, should another war occur. I should like to quote Hanson W. Baldwin, the well-known military authority, who states in the New York Times of March 20 this year:
Washington indicated last week that American atomic weapons might he used like bullets against military targets in case of communist aggression anywhere in the world. This doctrine of so-called limited atomic strategy was first enumerated by secretary of state Dulles and was immediately supported by President Eisenhower. It follows earlier decisions by the national security council and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
Taken collectively these decisions imply not an irrevocable and general decision to use atomic weapons under any and all circumstances, but it does show a very clear trend toward primary dependence upon atomic strategy.
We are told in the same article that in the United States the organization and tactics of the army, navy and air force are being changed to integrate these weapons into that country's offensive and defensive plans. For example, the United States army has already carried out tests of so-called atomic age divisions, both armoured and infantry, which streamline the present division, reducing it in size and making it more mobile, strengthening its communications and training it for quick dispersing and assembling.
The United States navy is also taking part in this development. They are commissioning at the present time two cruisers to be converted into guided missile ships. We are also told that the American air force is now organized and trained administratively and tactically, primarily for atomic war.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, in the light of these revolutionary developments by our good neighbour to the south, how can any conventional weapons program play anything but a minor role in the new strategy of warfare? Yet, according to the little information that has been made available, Canada continues to follow such an obsolete program.

Let us try to examine what type of weapons Canada is now producing. The white paper recently placed in our hands does not assist us a great deal on this score. But in the Canada Year Book of 1954 we find more specific information as to the type of weapons program we have been following. According to this source of information our major production project has been the 3-inch 50-calibre naval guns and mountings. Browning 0-5-inch machine guns were produced for use in Sabre and CF-100 jet fighters. There are 3-5-inch rocket launchers for use by the Canadian army.
Arrangements, apparently, have also been made to produce 155-millimetre and 105-millimetre howitzers, the 105-millimetre recoilless rifle and 81-millimetre and 60-millimetre mortars.
Contracts for small arms were limited mainly, I understand, because these weapons have not yet been standardized.
Ammunition requirements altered with the change-over to the United States types of equipment. This made Canada decide to produce ammunition for the army's 155-mm, 105-mm, and 90-mm artillery.
According to this same year book, naval requirements to be met from domestic sources include ammunition for 3-inch 50-calibre 40mm Bofors guns, depth charges. That indicates a very conventional weapons program carried out by our defence department especially in comparison with the new weapons developed by the United States such as nuclear depth charges for use at sea, atomic shells for use with 280-mm guns with a range of about 18 miles, atomic war-heads, the army's guided missile with a range of about 75 miles, atomic war-heads for antiaircraft and air-to-air missiles, as well as the war-heads for the Matador and Regulus pilotless bombers.
The recent tests in Nevada have added another milestone to the development of these modern weapons, making our Canadian program that much more obsolete. The tests the United States conducted there have led to the development of a whole family of fission and fusion, and combined fission-fusion weapons of different sizes and shapes, designed for many purposes.
Strangely enough, the United States has been giving out this information on the development of modern weapons while our government has given parliament almost no information at all on the progress of our defence, using the pretext of national security, when, in fact, national security was not involved. For example, in reply to questions by the member for Assiniboia as to whether
Supply-National Defence Canada possessed atomic weapons of any kind, the Minister of National Defence stated, at page 1643 of Hansard of March 2, 1955:
The first and second parts of this question, dealing respectively- with the possession by Canada and the transportation in Canada of atomic bombs and atomic weapons, obviously cannot be answered for security reasons.	.
Such an answer serves no purpose unless it is to hide the weakness of our defence policy. It is well known and very widely publicized that the United States, the United Kingdom and the Soviet union are producing such weapons, and they make no effort to hide the fact.
Our neighbours to the south seem to delight in an almost daily bulletin reporting the progress of atomic weapons. Even Great Britain, in its statement on defence last February, was quite outspoken when it stated that the United Kingdom also has the ability to produce such weapons, after commenting on thermonuclear weapons in possession of the United States and the Soviet governments:
After fully considering all the implications of this step, the government have thought it their duty to proceed with their development and production.
But here in Canada it is totally different, as indicated by the answer given by the Minister of National Defence. To me, it would appear that the minister's answer confirms what has long been suspected, namely, that Canada's defence program consists of conventional, or perhaps I should more appropriately say obsolete, weapons. It also indicates that we have not begun to adopt the new weapons and the new strategy for fighting in the new kind of war that we may be involved in.
This appears to me to be an extremely serious situation, if for no other reason than that, for the past four years, more than 40 per cent of our total budget expenditure has been for defence. If this government continues to spend such large amounts for weapons that will never be used in any war because of their obsolete nature, then it is guilty of wasting the Canadian taxpayers' money for which we get no return in the form of effective protection. Much of our expenditure has been just pure unadulterated waste.
It seems to me that the government are relying for protection on the great distance between us and our potential attackers, the U.S.S.R. I would, however, point out that distance is no longer protection because fast Russian planes have the ability and power to deliver these devastating explosives on any Canadian or United States target.

Supply-National Defence
In this connection, I would like to quote briefly from an article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen on May 17, this year, written by Stewart Alsop, of Washington. He deals with the reaction in the pentagon after Moscow's May-day celebration:
For what really shook the pentagon was the two formation flights of apparently fully operational B-52-type heavy bombers. This means that we are at best neck-and-neck in the race for the intercontinental jet bomber, which will certainly be the decisive factor in the air-atomic balance until the arrival of the intercontinental missile. And what shook the pentagon even more was the appearance of the entirely new all-weather fighter.
For the existence of such a plane argues the existence of an immensely complex weapons system of which an all-weather fighter is only a part, including early warning and ground control systems. The intelligence confirms the probable existence of a fully mature Soviet air defence (which this country will not have at least until the summer of 1957). Against a Soviet air defence built around all-weather fighters, this country's reserves of comparatively slow B-36 heavy bombers must be virtually written off as a factor in the air-atomic balance.
The author goes on to say:
But the most disturbing aspect of the situation is the technical brilliance displayed by the Soviet air engineers. Both the type 39 and the type 37 do the same jobs as our B-47's and B-52's with half the number of engines. This means that the Soviet engineers have developed jet engines with twice the thrust of any jet achieved in this country. Moreover, their B-52 type plane took just four years from drawing board to operational unit, whereas our B-52 took six and a half years.
This article furnishes further evidence of how obsolete our defence equipment is.
Despite the accelerated defence program in the last four years, in which more than $6J billion were spent on the defence services, the defence of Canada is totally ineffective and only just begun.
I would point out that some of the best informed military experts cast grave doubt on the validity of air or any other defence in the present era. The Canadian and American military experts appear to be convinced of the need for radar fighter screens. For the moment, let us look at what has been accomplished to date.
The only completed radar screen in existence is the "Pinetree" radar line which straddles the United States-Canadian border. It was begun in 1950 and, I understand, is now completed. Canada contributed one-third of its total $250 million cost but, for the life of me, I cannot see how it affords much defence to Canada since any attack from Russia would come from the north. Indeed, its effectiveness, even in terms of United States defence, is often seriously questioned.

Time magazine, of December 20, 1954, commenting on this particular radar line, warns that its 200-mile range provides very short notice of attack. The air defence command will not now guarantee any warning time at all.
Coastal radar runs from Vancouver to San Diego in the Pacific, from Labrador to Savannah on the Atlantic, with navy radar ships patrolling offshore for added warning.
Some radar nets have been built around critical targets and large cities but mostly the radar line is very thin and sometimes stations are closed for repairs.
Another point that was recently made by military critics is that the radars are beamed high for maximum range, leaving gaps for low level attack.
Canada is now in the process of building the mid-Canada line of small semi-automatic, electronic-detection stations along the 55th parallel which is roughly 500 miles north of the United States border. Only last fall did Canada and the United States jointly decide to construct a distant early warning radar line, the D.E.W. line. This will be some 1,800 miles north of Chicago and is far enough away to give a three-hour warning. But unfortunately it will be another two years or more before this line is completed.
If such significance is attached to radar fighter screens against attacking bombers, why is it that Canada is only now beginning to construct such a defence, although the defence program has been under way for more than four years? To make these radar lines effective there should be sufficient modern guided missile-equipped jet fighters. And yet, Mr. Dave Macintosh, writing in the Montreal Gazette on March 30 last, has this to say:
A high government source says the federal administration must decide before long whether Canada will supply the money and manpower for a huge air defence build-up in this country or whether American forces will be permitted into Canada to do the job.
Mr. Macintosh, continuing I presume with information from the same high government source, said that by the end of this year there will be only some 200 Canadian fighter planes CF-100 all-weather jets ready to meet an air attack on this continent.
To all Canadians who have been relying on the efficiency of the radar fighter screens to ward off attacks it must come as a real shock to learn that after all these years of defence building we have only one screen, "Pinetree", which provides little warning before western or eastern cities are under attack, and also that the two northern lines which will give more warning are still

far from being completed. Even when completed, the prospect of having sufficient modern Canadian planes to give them effect appears remote.
We in this group claim that the high level of defence spending cannot be justified because of the obsolete weapons that make up our defence program. 1 have not referred to the reserve army because the effectiveness of this body has been reduced to a minimum because of their still more extremely obsolete equipment.
The Canadian defence program was originally determined in 1950-51 by the requirements of NATO in meeting the possible aggression by communist forces in Europe. Therefore let us briefly review what NATO has accomplished from a military point of view in the last four years.
When General Eisenhower assumed command of SHAPE in early 1951, he had command of 15 active divisions. Today, four years later, these have grown to 46 divisions whose fire power is much greater than the fire power of the best equipped division in world war II. This is largely attributable to the new weapons provided by the United States. Added to this, West Germany will add another 12 active divisions within the next two years.
The build-up in NATO's air strength has been just as significant. In 1951 NATO had only a handful of planes, some of them of doubtful quality. Today NATO has approximately 6,000 fairly modern aircraft. Now that West Germany is a member of NATO it plans to contribute an additional 1,500 planes to this total.
Impressive as this build-up has been, it is overshadowed by even more spectacular achievements by most of the NATO countries themselves. The real potential power of NATO lies in the total forces at the disposal of its member nations not necessarily assigned to the NATO command.
In this connection I would point out that the defence expenditure of the fourteen NATO countries totalled less than $20 billion in 1949, but since 1953 they have averaged more than $60 billion a year.
Probably the most powerful protection against communist aggression is outside of NATO. I refer to the United States strategic air command with long-range B-47 stratojets able to carry atom and hydrogen bombs to any target in the U.S.S.R. It is under the direct control of President Eisenhower.
The strategic air command of the United States has wings of B-47 stratojets in Britain and Morocco. While not under NATO's command, they are available to support NATO 50433-308
Supply-National Defence in the event of an attack. Possibly this is the strongest force for peace in the world today.
The sense of urgency which was responsible for our defence program following the outbreak of war in Korea no longer applies; for in the interim period Russia has been completely encircled by American air bases, manned with air power capable of swift retaliation against aggression. Such precautions, to my mind, have reduced the chance of a major war almost to the vanishing point.
The facts that I have just mentioned clearly indicate that the optimum military build-up has been achieved. The massive military strength of NATO, together with the individual NATO countries and especially the United States, is, according to military authorities, many times greater in terms of destructive potential than was ever arrayed against Germany at the peak of the allied power in world war II.
In view of these accomplished facts, it is extremely difficult for me to understand why the Canadian government is maintaining approximately the same high level of defence expenditures that it undertook during the period of the crash program when the western defence situation was entirely different.
Even the United States has reduced its defence expenditures considerably more than Canada, as the following comparison will show. Peak spending in both countries was for the fiscal year 1952-53. That year the United States spent on defence $43-6 billion. For the fiscal year 1955-56 the United States plans to spend $34 billion, or a drop of 22 per cent.
On the other hand, Canada's defence expenditure was $1,846,916,817 in 1952-53, whereas for the current fiscal year, 1955-56, we have budgeted an amount of $1,729,285,194 for our defence services, or a drop of 6 per cent. If we had undertaken the same reduction in our defence spending as our neighbours to the south, our budget would be reduced by a further sum of close to $300 million.
We are convinced that this country could reduce its defence expenditures by $400 million without in any way impairing the effectiveness of our present defence program.
In view of the statement I have made, that we are still stockpiling obsolete equipment and materials-equipment that will never be used in any war-we strongly recommend that the government make sharp reductions in defence expenditure, particularly the moneys now being spent on obsolete equipment, and that a complete reappraisal of our defence program be undertaken in the light

Supply-National Defence of the development of a new kind of warfare for which our present defence program is totally inadequate.
Indeed, we are still producing equipment that has been on exhibition in war museums across the country for several years. In fact, we have sufficient museum pieces in our stockpiles to supply more than all the war museums in Canada require.
We of this group also recommend that a greater percentage of our defence appropriations be allocated for research work. Canada is lagging far behind other countries in this connection. The Hoover commission in the United States, in a recent report on the research and development work carried out by the defence department in that country, goes to the heart of the matter when it says:
The armed forces are not sufficiently daring and imaginative in their approach to radically new weapons and weapons systems.
The commission concludes that the pace for applying new scientific knowledge to weapons simply cannot be left to the informal proddings of civilian technologists. It urges the creation of a committee of outstanding scientists to work continuously and closely with the assistant secretary of defence for research and development.
While what I have read referred to the need for research in the United States-a country that has already developed a whole family of nuclear weapons-just think how much greater is the need for similar research in Canada at once.
Finally, I would suggest that the minister explore the possibilities of co-ordinating the activities of the reserve army and the civil defence units. In my opinion, this would enhance the morale of these units and of the public as these activities would be directly related to the defence needs of the local region and local population.
The time has arrived when parliament- that is, we common members-should take a more active interest in defence matters. To my mind, there is only one way in which this can be done, namely, by the establishment of a standing committee on defence expenditure.
In view of the fact that parliament, to date, has been so ill-informed with regard to defence matters, also because our defence expenditures comprise over 40 per cent of our total budget, it is imperative, to my mind, that such a committee be set up immediately, to be in operation for the next session of parliament. I hope the minister will take the suggestions I have made as being made in the same good faith as those made by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, with

a view to being critically helpful to the end that we may build up the greatest defence we can possibly afford for our common protection.
