Mr. Chairman, I should like to join with the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich in congratulating the minister on his appointment to the portfolio of defence. We realize that he has inherited a department which carries with it a tremendous amount of work and a tremendous amount of sacrifice. It is also a department which carries with it very little thanks. As a matter of fact, I think the Minister of National Defence takes more abuse and more criticism than does any other minister in the cabinet. While I am on the subject of congratulation I should like to do as I have done in the past and offer a word of congratulation to the armed forces of this country. Wherever they have gone, I think they have built up an enviable reputation, not only as fighting men but as men and gentlemen. They have always served with distinction in every field in which they have been engaged and in every battle in which they have fought. They have always been well known for their courage, their ability and their resourcefulness. In these times of at least partial peace I think that those in our services overseas have served as ambassadors of good will and have earned the friendship of people wherever they may be. I want to make it perfectly clear also that any criticisms I might have are directed not toward the personnel of the armed forces but toward the department and the policies of that department.
This morning the minister gave us a detailed survey. While I am on that matter, I might just ask the minister-as I did last year-whether he would consider, in future years, making his statement on one day and then adjourning the debate until the next day in order to give the members of the House of Commons the opportunity to make some sort of study of the subject matter of that statement. The minister spoke for about an hour this morning. He put forward a great deal of information. It is practically impossible for anyone to absorb all of it as it is being given and it is imperative that we have a fairly good understanding of what the minister is saying before we make any attempt to criticize or to comment on that statement. I offer that suggestion to the minister for what it is worth.
The minister indicated that the world situation and the tension is easing somewhat and that we probably now have a little bit more hope for peace than we have had in the near past. But let us face up to the fact that the situation is serious and that it will probably

continue to be serious for a good number of years. We hope-as does every member of the house and every person in this country- that we shall not be called upon to face another all-out war. But we always have that possibility hanging over our heads as long as the threat of communism is on the face of the earth.
As has been pointed out, any war between communism and the western democracies is different from any other war that has been fought. This is a battle between two ways of life: between communist dictatorship on the one hand and democracy on the other, between the forces of freedom and the forces of slavery. We must not under any circumstances be lulled by any peace overtures that are made by the communist countries. We must always remember that they have told us many times that world domination is their ultimate aim and that they will be satisfied with nothing else.
We certainly hope that the peace moves that have been made by the new regime in Russia in the last few years are sincere. But we must always keep in the back of our minds the fact that it has been made plain by the communists, ever since the days of Marx and Engels, that they intend to rule the world and to conquer it by one means or another. As I said, possibly the new administration in Russia has had some change in heart, some softening of attitude. We hope that they are sincere. But in the event that there is no sincerity, we believe that Canada should and must carry on a defence program to the very highest possible degree.
I think the minister will agree that we in this group have always supported defence spending in any amount that we felt was necessary for the conduct of our defence program. We have always done this and we shall continue to do so because it is allimportant. Any criticisms that we have had in the past or may have now or in the future come as a result of our disagreement with the handling of the department and the handling of the money rather than the spending itself. We think that the aims of the department are undoubtedly worthy but that the results sometimes leave much to be desired. We feel that, in many cases, the people of this country are not getting dollar value for the expenditures that are made. I think the defence expenditure committee that we had for two years in the last parliament did an inestimable job and proved that there were many ways in which the methods of spending defence moneys could be improved. In that regard I would urge the government to consider setting up the defence expenditure committee again early in the 50433-308J
Supply-National Defence next session so that we can continue the good work done by that committee during the two years of its existence.
I should like to join the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich and the minister in welcoming the Federal Republic of Germany into NATO. We think it means a whole lot more than the addition of a certain number of fighting men and equipment. It means that throughout the whole of western Europe we now have a unity among the people, a unity of aims, desires and defence. In my opinion it means a great deal, not only from the point of view of the manpower situation but with respect to the morale of all the peoples of the free world, to know that the Federal Republic of Germany has joined us and will give us the support that we feel we should get. In other words, the Federal Republic of Germany is now more than a buffer state. She is an ally and we welcome her.
There is one piece of information I should like to get from the minister. I know there is no possible way of obtaining the actual figures but no doubt approximate figures are available. I believe NATO headquarters have issued statements from time to time on the approximate strength of the Russian land, sea and air forces. I think such figures were put on the record in 1953, and if it is possible for the minister to do so I should like him to bring the figures up to date so that we can make some comparison, see the headway that the NATO countries are making in their defence projects, whether or not our defence program is sufficient and whether or not we are doing all that we should be doing in the name of security.
The minister said so much this morning that I had trouble trying to follow it all, but I think he said that we were maintaining our productive superiority as far as the arms race is concerned. I hope that is so. We must remember that Soviet Russia does have a tremendous productive potential. Unlike the western nations, Russia is not too interested in how well her own people are getting along, and they are quite willing to sacrifice the needs and wishes of their own people in order to advance their defence productive effort. I hope the minister is right in believing that we are maintaining productive superiority over the Soviet union and its satellites.
In referring to air attack on Canada, the minister indicated this morning that there was no sure defence against an atomic attack. I can certainly agree with him on that point. In my opinion we have too few industrial centres in Canada. That brings me to a point that has been raised on many occasions, the decentralization of industry. I think

Supply-National Defence that a dozen atomic bombs dropped on strategic positions in Canada could practically wreck our entire economy. The tact that could happen emphasizes the need for decentralization of our industries and spreading them throughout Canada so that there will not be such a small number of strategic targets. I would hate to see an atomic attack on Toronto or Montreal. Two attacks, one on each of these cities, would cripple us tremendously. In my opinion the minister and the government should consider strongly placing more of our defence construction and production in the maritimes, throughout the prairies and all across the country.
We must under no circumstances become complacent and feel that we are not going to be attacked but that if we are we can continue to carry on. The "it can't happen here" complex is a very dangerous thing, and I suggest that the only way we can overcome any concentrated A-bomb or H-bomb attack is by the absolute decentralization of our war industry. The question of decentralization also brings up a matter that has been mentioned in years past and debated many times in the house. In a day when warfare involves highly mobile and fast-moving fighting units, we definitely need a trans-Canada highway system across the country for the transportation of troops to any part of the country in a short time. We need a highway system that could substitute for our rail system in the event of our major rail centres being bombed. I do not refer simply to a trans-Canada highway but a trans-Canada highway system which would probably mean three or four trans-Canada highways right across the country, including, of course, the Yellowhead route to which many members have referred in the past.
On page 7 of the white paper the minister mentions that the navy now has 154 ships in commission, but I notice that of that number there are only 22 which can be considered first-line ships. Of that number nine are frigates which, unless they have been radically redesigned and re-equipped, would be absolutely inefficient so far as present-day anti-submarine operations are concerned. Twenty-two ships would of course give us something like three convoy escort groups. As the minister has often said, we would be primarily an escort or convoy navy.
I suggest to the minister it would be extremely unwise for us to allow our first-line ships to become so few that we could not handle more than three convoys going across the ocean. This morning the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich said that he could not see us convoying troops across the Atlantic in the same way as we did in world war II.

I took him to mean that he was presuming that maybe the next attack would be made on this continent. If that is so we would need our convoys not to take troops from this side over to Europe but to bring troops and supplies from Europe to this country, and I do not think that under any circumstances we should allow the strength of our first-line escort vessels to deteriorate. We must keep them up under any circumstances.
I should like to make an appeal again to the minister, as I have done in past years, to consider the construction of what, in the second -world war, we used to call merchant aircraft carriers. Without those small converted aircraft carriers, I doubt very much if we could have won the battle of the Atlantic. Many, many times those small reconnaissance planes took off from the decks of these carriers and discovered wolf packs of submarines far in advance of the convoy. We were able to dispose of them before the convoy went by. I cannot think of any cheaper way of assuring the safe conduct of a convoy across the Atlantic than by the conversion of some of these merchant ships into carriers that will carry a small, light plane capable of submarine reconnaissance. They did a marvellous job during world war II, and I see no reason why they could not continue to do just as effective a job under present conditions.
I want to say one word about the acquisition of submarines from the Royal Navy. I sincerely hope that the only purpose of those submarines is to train Canadian personnel. I would hope that the Department of National Defence would not consider trying to build up an operational fleet of submarines. I do not think they are necessary. We have a definite job to carry out in naval warfare and I do not believe the placing of men on submarines would further our defence effort in any way. So far as training exercises are concerned, it is the only way the personnel of the navy can be properly trained. I realize that. I have worked with some of the Royal Navy submarines during the war, and gained a great deal of invaluable experience as a result of those training exercises.
No matter how hard you try to simulate a submarine search it is impossible to get the real feel of it until you are working with an actual submarine. I do congratulate the minister on bringing these submarines over to train with the Canadian fleet. They are needed, and the training exercises we will get with those submarines will certainly be an asset to the Canadian navy. Under no circumstances, however, could I agree that Canada should ever have any submarines for operational work.

I should like now to mention the air defence plan to which reference was made by both previous speakers, our radar screens and our air support plan. I am going to agree with both previous speakers that, although the radar screens when completed will be an asset to the Canadian defence effort, I also agree that I do not believe we have the air power to back up any warnings we might get of mass air attacks across the polar regions. I wonder if we could stop a squadron or two of hostile enemy bombers before they could do a tremendous amount of damage to the productive capacity of this country. A while ago the minister mentioned that a great deal of experimental work was being conducted with guided missiles. He mentioned both air-to-air and air-to-ground missiles with which the Canadian forces were dealing.
I would suggest to the minister that is not the proper way of going about it. I would think that in view of the tremendous waste tracts across our north, and the fact there is a possibility of air attack across the north, it might be advisable if we were to specialize on ground-to-air guided missiles rather than the others. Such missile bases could be placed somewhere near the early warning lines and used to attack any bombing force which might endanger this country. 1 cannot think of a cheaper or a more reasonable way of assuring our safety against air attack than the use of these ground-to-air missiles.
One more thing, Mr. Chairman. I should like to agree with the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes) in his plea that the reserve units of this country be trained for civil defence. I feel it would be of great value to this country to have a group of men who are well trained and who could be mobile, to handle any emergency that might arise in the event of attack on this country. These men would be gathered in every large centre and could be moved to any other centre where their services were needed to supplement the civil defence portion that they have in most cities. It would be wonderful training for them. In addition, it would give the people of Canada a good deal of reassurance to know that trained civil defence personnel would be available as well as the civil defence people who are trained in these various cities.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that many times in the last couple of years we have heard reports over the air or seen them in the newspapers that someone in the armed forces has been killed in an aircrash or an accident at some training establishment and the names are being withheld until the next of kin have been notified.
Supply-National Defence I know that the reason for withholding the names is undoubtedly to ensure that the department is the party that notifies the next of kin. This prevents the neighbours hearing the news over the air and running over with the story. But I wonder how kind that whole procedure is? It may be protecting the feelings of the next of kin, but how much agony is being caused to the relatives of servicemen who are at the base from which the report comes?
I have known of cases where accidents have occurred, shall we say, at Gimli or Camp Borden, and people who had boys at those establishments suffered the agonies of the damned while they were waiting to find out whether or not their boy had been involved in the accident. I am wondering if the minister could not ask the co-operation of the news services in withholding reports of fatal accidents until such time as the next of kin have been notified, because I think it is a shame that so many people should have to suffer from lack of knowledge in order to protect the next of kin of the boy who was killed. I do not suggest any type of censorship; I do not think that would be the answer. I think the news services would be glad to co-operate in withholding that news until such time as the next of kin had been notified. Then, the names could be published along with the news story clear across the country without causing worry to so many people across this country. I should like the minister to consider that phase of it, because I have felt very strongly in the matter. I have had many people mention to me, when they have heard this news, "I wonder if it is my boy who has been killed." It is a matter involving only a few hours, and surely the government and the news services could co-operate in withholding that information for the number of hours necessary to notify the next of kin.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to join with hon. members who have preceded me in congratulating the Minister of National Defence upon the statement he delivered this morning. To me it was the most comprehensive statement on defence affairs we have had in the House of Commons for a number of years. Unfortunately, for security reasons, with which I have no quarrel, he could not give us all the details we want.
The defence of Canada and defence matters generally have been the subject of public attention in the last three or four years, and particularly in the last three or four weeks. The fear of atomic and H-bombs has brought to the attention of the public as never before the need for the defence of the people in this country.

Supply-National Dejence
I do not want to enter into a discussion of one service as against another, but I should like for a few moments to deal with one or two aspects of the naval service, and possibly the army, and then I shall confine my remarks chiefly to the air force.
At page 6 of the white paper under the heading "Royal Canadian Navy" the minister has this to say:
On the west coast the 2nd minesweeping squadron and a reserve training squadron were formed last year.
. There is no mention in this white paper as to what reserve squadron or what minesweeping squadron we have on the Atlantic. I would ask the minister to give that information, if he can, when he replies.
Much has been said today about the need for Canada's defence. I believe we will all agree that the first duty of the government and of every member in the house is the defence of Canada and the protection of her people. Mention has been made by one or two previous speakers about the Atlantic, and I wish to touch on that subject because I come from an Atlantic province.
As hon. members are no doubt aware, the last war was very nearly lost on the Atlantic, and it was just touch and go as to whether we would win. No one has paid greater tribute than has Sir Winston Churchill to the work of our naval and air forces, which contributed to the victory on the Atlantic. In his war memoirs he was most emphatic in saying that if we had lost the battle of the Atlantic we would have lost the war.
In the last three or four years I have drawn the attention of the house to the need for protecting our convoys on the Atlantic. I have drawn the attention of hon. members to the up to date submarines the Russians possess, and the doubtful defences we have to combat those modern submarines. I would not want to say anything in the house that would give comfort to the Russians or to any potential enemy. I do want to say, however, that three or four years ago manoeuvres took place between Bermuda and Newfoundland in which 14 surface vessels were pitted against three submarines. Quoting from a memorandum appearing in the New York Times of that date it was demonstrated that at the close of this exercise all 14 vessels had been destroyed, though they had not even contacted one of the three submarines.
I believe that since that time we have developed better devices to combat the submarine menace; but I have seen nothing and I know of nothing even up to this time which would lessen that danger. It must be kept in mind that I come from a province which is open to submarine attack, and that to

obtain supplies the shipping lanes must be kept open. Two or three enemy submarines around the coast of Newfoundland would close off supplies completely. In this event Canada would be placed in the position that she would have to supply Newfoundland by air. That is a possibility that must be taken into consideration, and I stress it here today.
We know about the submarine menace in Newfoundland because we had submarine warfare right at our front door. We feel strongly about it because it was brought home to us with great force. With this in mind I advocate now, not in any political sense whatsoever but strictly from a knowledge of our requirements as a province of Canada, the building of another airport in Newfoundland. Whether it be a joint effort between Canada and the United States or an effort on our part alone is immaterial. Such airports should be built, however, to take care of the air traffic which will flow back and forth across the Atlantic in the event of hostilities. This is a vital necessity. Gander, big as it is, cannot handle the traffic. Harmon Field cannot handle it; neither can Torbay; neither can Goose.
The possibilities involved should be taken into consideration immediately, and I believe our American friends would be receptive to the suggestion. While stalled at Gander for 24 hours some two or three years ago because of weather conditions I discussed the possibility of increasing the facilities, as I have indicated, and it was urged upon me by many people there. Just as Gander was established before the last war to take care of the possibilities the British saw coming, I say we must now take into consideration the building of another airport to take care of the air traffic. It would be too late to make such arrangements after hostilities began. That is all I am going to say on the subject of airports.
Mention has been made of the need for greater protection for our convoys. May I say to the hon. member who last spoke that convoy protection by air during the last war was carried out principally from Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Iceland and Northern Ireland. Our bombers, having a greater range, permitted us to have cover from Halifax right across the Atlantic. I have one suggestion to add, and it is that we need not only closer protection than we had before, but we shall need protection for convoys in all kinds of weather. This cannot be supplied from the points I have just mentioned. May I suggest to the Royal Canadian Navy, in all humility, that what we need are helicopters to be carried on the decks of merchant ships, from which they can take off,

go aloft and land. These helicopters could give air protection to convoys when weather conditions were bad and when the long-range bombers from Newfoundland and other places would not be able to afford that protection. In my opinion that is a necessity. As I said, I offer the suggestion in all humility. I believe it could be carried out at very limited expense, and that preparations should be made for it.
I do not want to get into any controversy as to which of the services should have priority. I believe that in the last two or three weeks irresponsible statements, which do not make for partnership in the services, have been made in the press. When one reads that the army should be abolished entirely and all our efforts devoted to the air force, one wonders just why such statements are made.
There is no doubt about it; under modern conditions the army has a limited role to play. There is no doubt that the air force is the predominant force in Canada today; but to say that the army is finished, that it is obsolete and useless, is going too far. The army will have a part to play, even if it is only a subsidiary one. I say that quite frankly. I said it here four years ago. If any priority is to be given to one service it must be given to the air force. I said that four years ago, and it is more evident today than ever before.
I hold in my hand a book entitled "Air Power and National Security", from which I should like to quote a few passages. The parts I wish to quote bear out the point I am trying to make. Usually I do not quote very much. The reason I am quoting today is that I find the quotations in this book very pungent and very apropos of the times in which we live. The writers of these articles have put their points in much better language than I could. Let me quote from an article "Some Fallacies concerning Air Power":
In the air are no streets, no channels, no point where one can say of an antagonist, "If he wants to reach my capital he must come by here." In the air all directions lead everywhere.
And again:
It must seem strange that the sky, too, is about to become another battlefield no less important than the battlefields on land and sea. But from now on we had better get accustomed to this idea and prepare ourselves for the new conflicts to come.
The struggle for the command of the air will be bitter; and the so-called civilized nations will strive to forge the most telling means to wage the conflict.
I think we have reached that stage today. For the first time in the history of Canada and the United States we are vulnerable to
Supply-National Defence attack from the air. That is the opinion of military-minded people today, and also of civilians who follow this reasoning. Today air power will either win or lose a war. We could not have won the war of 19391945 if we had not air predominance. The battle of the Pacific was decided by air power. Japan was brought to her knees by air power. We could not have landed on the Normandy beaches if we had not air power and a predominance over the enemy.	This air predominance finally
brought down Germany. It is more important today.
Air power is more in evidence today than ever before because of the hydrogen and atomic bombs. We are living in fear of a nuclear war which threatens us today, and every precaution must be taken to guard ourselves against it. We have no defence against it except the warning lines we are building and our own air force, and possibly guided missiles.
It is a recognized fact that if the enemy attacks us in force a certain proportion of his bombers will get through. If they carry the hydrogen bomb it will take very few bombs to destroy the war potential of this continent. That is the danger under which we live, and we have to face it whether we like it or not. Therefore when we are appropriating money for the services we must of necessity give priority to the air force. We must build up our defences so we can protect our cities and our inhabitants against this potential attack.	There is no doubt
about that in the minds of those who have spoken here today, and there is certainly no doubt in my mind that this potential for destruction faces us today as never before.
May I quote further from this book. During the first war Great Britain set up a commission to study air power. This commission was set up in 1916-1917 by Mr. Lloyd George, who was then prime minister. The head of the commission was the late Field Marshal Jan Smuts. In the official report, which was called by some the magna carta of British air power, we find the following:
The day may not be far off when aerial operations with their devastation of enemy lands and destruction of industrial and populous centres on a vast scale may become the principal operations of war to which the older forms of military and naval operations may become secondary and subordinate.
It is important that we should not only secure air predominance, but secure it on a very large scale; and having secured it in this war (1914-18) we should make every effort and sacrifice to maintain it for the future. Air supremacy may in the long run become as important a factor in the defence of the empire as sea supremacy.

Supply-National Defence
Further on it says:
For good or ill, air mastery is today the supreme expression of military power, and fleets and armies, however necessary and important, must accept subordinate rank. This is a memorable milestone in the march of men.
That statement was made by Sir Winston Churchill when he spoke in Boston in 1949. It was seen by men of vision and men who looked toward the future. The thing we have to remember, so far as this world is concerned, is the dominance of air power. Since we have developed the atom bomb and the hydrogen bomb the powers of destruction have increased tremendously. We have to take every precaution we possibly can to keep such bombers away from our shores. It will be too late when it happens. Military strategists say that whoever gets in the first bombing attack will do much to win the war. In talking about home defence and beyond that, the white paper says on page 4:
We are also assisting in the protection of the industrial potential of North America and the retaliatory capacity of the United States strategic air force, both of which are of the greatest significance to all nations in the free world in the deterrence of aggression.
The only force the free nations have to deter aggression is the United States strategic air force. I am glad the minister put those remarks in the white paper and said we are assisting in the development of that strategic air force about which we have heard so much and about which so much comment has been made in the capitals of different countries. The potential enemy has been getting his propaganda going, decrying the potential retaliatory effects of the United States strategic air force.
Along with many people I believe that if we did not have this strategic air force we would not be in a position to talk to Russia on anything like equal terms. Second, we would not be in the position in which we have been lately in seeing Russia take counsel of her fears regarding this air force and meeting together in conference with our statesmen to work out some conclusions for peace.
Since the Austrian peace treaty, Russia has gone to Yugoslavia, and has extended an invitation to Chancellor Adenauer to visit Russia. All this has come about because of the air power we have. We are in a position to hit back, and that is the only thing deterring the Russians today. It is the greatest guarantee we have today for peace in the world. I shall elaborate on the statement of the minister by quoting from this book again:
Today we live in an age in which force has become the determining factor in international relations. Wars that once were considered a contest between professional groups and forces, suddenly have completed the evolution to total

war between civilizations. Air power has broken down cultural and national barriers and becomes increasingly important in everyday life.
In other words we are living in a time of total war.
The future-peace or chaos-is man's choice. Within one hour of detecting red bombers in free-world skies, the west's nuclear-armed strategic bombers would begin taking off from bases all over the world, hundreds of them, with one destination -Russia. Attacking Soviet aircraft would find the west's bases empty. No international conferences, not even a quick general staff meeting. The gun is loaded. It is as automatic as pushing a button. It could take even less to set it off; an accident, for example. An unavoidable risk.
That is the power we hold to deter Russia or China or anyone else from starting a third world war. It is our great safety valve, and we must support it by every means in our power.
This is the ability of the west. It is costly. It is unavoidable. For until the politics of reason finds the way to peace in the world, the politics of power is the only known means of a stalemate. The central force of that power today is air power.

subtopic: FAILURE TO PARTICIPATE IN CONTINENTAL TEST
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is the first opportunity we have had during the current session to discuss at any length the problems of defence. Already the minister and others who have spoken have given full emphasis to the importance of this subject to every Canadian and to all people living in the western world. So far as we in this house are concerned, we have the responsibility not only of attempting to assure in every Way we can as members of the House of Commons the maximum efficiency of our armed forces to meet whatever responsibility they must accept, but also to make sure in every way we can that the money spent on national defence is well spent and to the best effect. Some $2 billion goes from the public treasury to meet the requirements of this single department; therefore we must look at this both from the point of view of the effectiveness of our defence and the possibility of any practical economy which would be consistent with the demands made upon us.
I do not think it is necessary to emphasize that we all proceed from the same basic assumption in dealing with this matter. On whatever side of the house we may sit, and to whatever party we may belong, there can be no difference about our desire to see that our defence forces are as effective as possible and that those who are in the uniform of those forces are well trained, are well treated, have a feeling of confidence in their leadership and also have the assurance that they will be as well equipped as it is within the power of this nation to equip them.

However, it would be inconsistent and in fact it would be a neglect of duty for any hon. member of this house to refrain from making any comment which may be directed to the increase of efficiency and effectiveness, or to withhold any criticism that may appear appropriate in relation to any aspect of this great problem.
Before I proceed to deal with national defence as it has been set before us today and as it has been outlined in the white paper, I wish to deal with a subject which has been under discussion and which was mentioned in the house as recently as yesterday. It is necessary that it be mentioned because of the way a recent announcement was made which was designed to create uncertainty in the minds of the people of Canada generally and those in the armed forces particularly, in regard to certain steps that had been taken by the Department of National Defence.
It is only natural when discussions of this kind arise that there can be misunderstandings about what is at issue. May I make it perfectly clear that there can be no question about the right and duty of the government to decide what officer shall occupy any particular position at any time. If there is one principle that should not be changed it is the supremacy of the executive over the armed forces and the right and duty of the government of the day to determine what course will be followed, what plans will be made and what political decisions are appropriate, using the word "political" in its widest sense.
It would not be appropriate nor would it be in keeping with the best traditions of the armed forces if we were to precipitate a debate in this house in regard to the comparative merits of any officers of the armed forces. However, that does not preclude the desirability of making sure that whatever is done in connection with members of the armed forces is done in a way that neither creates unnecessary uncertainty in the mind of the public nor in any way creates an atmosphere of uncertainty in the minds of those in the armed forces about the way in which decisions are made.
The announcement a short time ago of the retirement of the chief of the general staff was no ordinary decision. It came at a time when there had been a good deal of speculation about various questions which had been disturbing the government; it came at a time when the government itself had taken under consideration certain statements that had been made; it came at a time when the role of senior officers in the matters under public 50433-309
Supply-National Defence discussion was very much in the thoughts of the members of the House of Commons as well as of the public generally.
That being so, it was most desirable that when an announcement was to be made that could only cause speculation, an explanation should have been given to the members of this house and through the press gallery to the public, which would have avoided any uncertainty. There was also a precedent because the very day before the announcement was made with regard to the retirement of the chief of the general staff, it had been regarded as desirable to make a statement in the House of Commons with regard to certain other matters under consideration.
It is perfectly true that the statement made was in response to certain comments which had been made in the house. Also, of course, questions have been raised in the House of Commons with regard to the circumstances under which the announcement was made with regard to the chief of the general staff. The point I made when this happened was, first of all, that while the house is sitting it is important that hon. members have these important subjects explained to them; and second, that the explanations given shall be understandable explanations which in themselves do not create further uncertainty.
I submit that the statement that the retirement of the chief of the general staff was merely in the course of ordinary rotation of appointments is hardly adequate under the circumstances. General Simonds is unquestionably the outstanding field officer produced by Canada during the last war. That was a matter of common agreement amongst senior officers in Canada, the United Kingdom, the United States and other allied countries. That being so, there was in the minds of hon. members a natural question as to why the services of a man who is still comparatively young, who is in the full vigour of excellent physical condition, and who has a great accumulation of experience, were not being employed in one of the several posts where skill of that kind and the experience he had acquired could be made use of in full measure.
There is no suggestion that anything General Simonds may have said at any time is in issue on this occasion. That cannot be so. Any of the things he has said which have perhaps had some controversial content were said sufficiently long ago that they could not possibly be the basis of the action which has just been taken. I think that consideration should be borne in mind. The government would have been remiss if they had not acted much earlier, if in fact their decision was in any way related to anything said by this very distinguished officer on an earlier occasion,

Supply-National Defence whether or not the government or anybody on this side of the chamber may disagree with what he said. After all, he would not be the first senior officer who has made statements that perhaps have gone slightly beyond the bounds of rigid military restraint. I think there have been cases when Field Marshal Montgomery has been known to make statements which went slightly beyond the narrow limits ordinarily imposed on senior officers in such a position.
Unquestionably such statements can be and are embarrassing. The best way to avoid that situation is to make perfectly clear what statements can and cannot be made. If any embarrassment has been caused by any statement made by any officer, I submit that the government itself must accept responsibility for the situation which has developed. On too many occasions it has encouraged, from senior officers as well as from senior civil servants, statements which would be helpful when certain subjects were being discussed. When encouragement or silent acquiescence leaves the impression that statements of that nature are welcome, it is only natural that they are bound to proceed from one stage to another and ultimately become embarrassing to the government itself.
Some of those statements-I am not referring to General Simonds in this case- undoubtedly have been embarrassing to the government. I would suggest, however, that the government look back over some statements that have exceeded the bounds of proper restraint which have been made and which were employed with some measure of satisfaction by the government when subjects of a controversial nature were under consideration in this House of Commons and elsewhere.
I suggest that the way to avoid anything of that kind in future is to have a clear understanding that senior officers should confine their remarks to the discussion of the non-political aspects of military affairs. I suggest that this can be done without any implied criticism of any officer; because if criticism is due, I repeat that I believe that criticism should be directed to the government itself which has encouraged the situation. Clear instructions along that line will avoid future embarrassment either to the government or to any officers. Also instructions to the effect that the government no longer encourages statements by unnamed or "highly reliable" sources would be very helpful. How often have we had read statements in the press from "reliable sources" dealing with some subject that is under active


discussion at the time. It is not possible to deal with those statements because no name is attached.
We had one of those statements just the day before yesterday. I repeat what I said before. Whether orally or in writing, a statement was certainly given to the Canadian Press, because the Canadian Press is not in the habit of giving in quotes statements that are a figment of somebody's imagination. There may be uncertainty about statements that are simply speculative reports, but I do not think there is one of us who believes that the Canadian Press, with its great traditions, would place in exact quotes statements of some military official unless they had received them from a military official to whom they had reason to look for an authoritative statement.
I can only express regret that the minister's inquiries brought him so little information. I even wonder whether he was as persistent as he might have been in his inquiries, because there are those who are rather under the impression that they have an idea where that statement came from. Perhaps a little further inquiry would inform the minister as to where that statement came from. I realize that it perhaps would not be appropriate to ask the Canadian Press from whom it came, because they undoubtedly were following a practice that has grown up. However, I think it would be a healthy thing if the words of the Prime Minister were observed, when he said the day before yesterday that he greatly deprecated statements of this kind given without the name of the person making the statement.
It should be understood that this will not be repeated, and that instructions will be given to that effect. There should be clear instructions to senior officers, as well as to senior civil servants, that while their statements are welcomed with regard to the subjects with which they are well acquainted, it is not appropriate for them at any time to cross into the realm of what are regarded as political decisions by a government.
Before I leave this subject, may I simply express the hope that General Simonds' training will be used in some capacity where it will be available to the public. It is not enough to say that a young officer at the age of 52 now automatically comes to the point of retirement. Other officers have continued in employment of different kinds. General McNaughton, who was at one time chief of the general staff, has been in the public service in different capacities for many years. General Foulkes on his retirement as chief of the general staff became the chairman of the chiefs of staffs committee. General

Worthington, who was not a chief of the general staff but a very distinguished staff officer, has been in the public service in different capacities since then.
I only mention these as examples. I would point out that the younger an officer is, the more reason there is to employ his services. After all, there is a very practical, material aspect to this. We are informed that General Simonds' pension will be in excess of $10,000 a year. His life expectancy would be in the neighbourhood of 25 years. That is a substantial sum involved in pension payments. Therefore both from the point of view of his skill and from the point of view of the two-thirds of whatever is paid by way of pension which will come out of the public treasury, because officers pay approximately one-third, I think we should all hope that the opportunity will be sought to use his highly skilled services in some capacity. In any event, I know all hon. members will join in expressing their admiration for the high standard of service which has always characterized General Simonds' service in the armed forces.
I want to deal now with the white paper even more than with the statements that have been made today, because the fact is that the minister's statements have not added anything to what he has placed before us in the white paper. He did emphasize again today a statement made in the white paper which reads as follows:
. . . appraisals of new weapons, new tactical and strategic concepts, and demands for increased mobility and flexibility of forces make it evident that changes in emphasis must be made from time to time within the defence programs of the NATO member nations.
Then the white paper goes on to say on page 4:
During the past year the United States has made considerable progress in the production of atomic and thermonuclear weapons. The U.S.S.R., after carrying out hydrogen bomb tests, has indicated that production of a stockpile of nuclear bombs is under way. More recently the government of the United Kingdom has announced its decision to proceed with the development and production of thermonuclear weapons.
Then I quote paragraph 7 on page 4:
For North America the possibility appears for the first time of an attack that could cripple the military and industrial potential of Canada and the United States. Should we ever be attacked with thermonuclear weapons, it is plain that our immediate problem would be national survival. Everyone not directly involved in an urgent military role would immediately be caught up in the problems of rescue, rehabilitation, and the maintenance of essential services.
It seems, Mr. Chairman, that this ominous and forceful statement with regard to the circumstances with which we are now confronted will not be seriously challenged by 50433-309}
Supply-National Defence any hon. member. I ask hon. members, however, if the statements in the white paper or in the house seem consistent with the warning given, and particularly with the emphasis on the need for appraisal of new weapons, new tactical and strategic concepts. All our thinking about defence has been changed by recent events. Now we know that we may be attacked here in our own homeland. That has created the fundamental change which the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich pointed out this morning, and the younger members of the house may not fully recognize the change.
In the days before the first world war even the remote possibility of an attack on the North American continent was never contemplated. The whole idea of military organization and preparation was based on the idea that Canadian forces would be a segment of European continental forces. Our divisional organization contemplated our participation in an army organization that might be engaged on the European continent.
In very large measure that frame of mind continued after the first world war. As has already been pointed out, there was not much difference in the general organization of the units employed in the great battles of the first world war and the units employed in the second world war, except for the enormous changes in equipment and in the emphasis, to some extent, on certain types of weapons.
Until quite recently, and in fact still, in the minds of many people there is the thought of large mass formations of which we form simply an integral segment. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that to an extent we have not yet been prepared to accept it as necessary for us to break away from that idea and have a distinctly Canadian concept of the organization of defence forces. We are the third largest nation in area in the world. Only China and Russia are larger.
Russia, with a land area nearly twice ours, has a population of some 220 million people. China, with nearly 500 million people, is only a little larger than Canada. We are the third largest land area with 15 million people. It is unwise and impractical for us to approach the problems of military and defence organization generally from the point of view of countries in Europe of the same population but with very small land areas, or of countries such as Britain, France, Germany, Italy or any of the other European countries with larger populations but with land areas only a small fraction of ours.

Supply-National Defence
Surely if our thoughts are now directed to the defence of Canada and our participation primarily in the defence of the North American continent as part of a general defence plan, then our thoughts should be directed to the method by which we can, with the utmost speed, bring to bear whatever military power is necessary at any given point, whether it be by air forces, by units of the army or by naval units, It is obvious that a country the size of Canada already so dependent on air transport through much of its great, developing north, cannot hope to provide the necessary military services by any conventional method.
This does not mean the abandonment of conventional forces. When it was said not long ago that we would be better off if the army disappeared entirely and those now in the army were put in the air force, I wonder if there may not have been a misinterpretation of what was said, or perhaps even the speaker may not have made sufficiently clear what he really intended.
There is some confusion in many people's minds between the air forces and forces carried by aircraft. Already today the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich has pointed out to us the immense importance of extreme mobility for all our armed services. I believe Canada should have a type of army organization that is unique in the world today. I believe our enormous land area and our small population call for the organization of an army in which every single unit will be airborne.
Suppose, for the sake of argument, there was a landing of paratroops at the radium mine on Great Bear lake. It would not be much use to start planning for the movement of land forces by train to Edmonton, then from Edmonton to the railhead on the Peace river, and from there by boat down the Mackenzie and across the Great Bear river to Great Bear lake. This would be a long, tedious and ineffective movement of armed forces.
The kind of armed forces we would need for a situation of that kind would be the type of units that could be transported immediately-when I say "immediately" I mean exactly that-to Great Bear lake where the necessary units made up of such services as would be required for the task could deal with whatever forces had been reported by wireless at that particular point.
The same thing would be true at the mouth of the Mackenzie, at the mouth of the Coppermine, on Hudson bay, over in the mines in eastern Quebec or in Labrador, at Whitehorse or anywhere in the Yukon.


If we were to deal with such a situation we would have to have extremely mobile, hard-hitting infantry, engineers, medical services, artillery units and other forces that could be moved without delay by great transport planes which can now carry units of that kind.
Let no one be in any doubt that transports adequate for that task already exist. At Farnborough last September I saw the new Blackburn transport actually carry two 25-pounder field guns and all the essential equipment that went with them. I also saw a fully loaded lorry driven into that huge transport. Whether or not that is the appropriate design, the fact is that transports of a size adequate for the purpose of carrying tanks, armoured vehicles, artillery weapons or anything of that kind are now available. They could be obtained or built here in the aircraft factories we already possess.
I would go so far as to say that this should apply not only to the permanent army but to the militia as well. I do not believe we have had enough information placed before us concerning the present position of the militia. It is far from satisfactory. The enlistments do not tell the story. The number of men on the roll do not tell you how effective militia training is. It is the number of days trained and the number of those trained at local headquarters who go to camp that measure the effectiveness of our militia units. Under all the circumstances it is really remarkable that our militia units have retained the keenness which has been shown by the officers, N.C.O.'s and men who have been training.
I do hope no hon. member is under the impression that our military training today is adequate, or that our military units are training in the way they should train in the face of the kind of emergency which has been impressed upon us by the Minister of Defence Production in the past few days. Let us take the case of artillery units which must train at camp if their training on the guns is to be really effective. Throughout Canada this year the average regiment of three batteries will not train more than one battery at camp. That is far from a satisfactory situation, at a time when we are told that we must contemplate the necessity of being prepared to meet an urgent situation of this kind.
In substantial measure the same is true of the training of other units, particularly units of a technical nature which require skill in handling vehicles and instruments of various kinds. The minister has mentioned figures that apply to the permanent force. We have before us also figures relating to the militia. Mr. Chairman, those figures have a meaning that can be interpreted in practical

terms only if, with the militia units, we are told accurately what training those units have which would fit them to accept the responsibilities that might be imposed upon them in a very short time, in the event of difficulties.
Much has been said about the problem of manning these units. Much has been said about the problem of raising the necessary manpower for the different branches of the service. I am convinced that the thing which will best assure an adequate enlistment in the different branches of our service-particularly the militia, which is still the backbone of our general training and which must be the pool from which a permanent force in the end will always be drawn-is to give to the training a sense of reality which it does not possess today. Give to the young men in the infantry, in the armoured force, in the engineers, in the artillery, in the army service corps, in the medical service, in the reconnaissance units and in the other units of our army, the knowledge that they are really taking part in a modern, up to date force, and you will see them flocking to the units in the way they have done on other occasions.
I do not believe there is any difference in the attitude of our young people toward the military services. Like many other hon. members in the house I can recall times when our problem, upon going to camp, was not that of not having enough men but what we would do with the extra men we found on the train when we were leaving for camp. And I can tell you there was a lot of very ingenious work done in order to work that out without too much financial strain on the officers involved.
That was actually the problem, and the reason was very simple. There was a sense of reality. I am speaking with direct knowledge of the artillery more than of any other branch of the service; but what 1 say with regard to the artillery was equally true in regard to other branches of the service. One of the main reasons for the desire of young men to go to camp with those units was the opportunity for competitive firing and competitive training; and that competition was between all units in the whole of Canada. The spirit of competition appealed greatly to young men and they really worked to win one of the numerous prizes open to units right across Canada. It was very noticeable that the units which won most of the prizes were those with the largest enlistment.
Unfortunately, though it is now ten years after the last war, competitive firing of that
Supply-National Defence kind has not been instituted in the artillery; nor has similar competitive training been instituted in the other branches of the armed services. This is the kind of thing that appeals to our young people. Give them a sense of reality. Give them a sense of competition between the units, and I think you will see plenty of young men enlisting in those units and the problem of manpower met adequately and satisfactorily in that way. You will find the young men anxious to take part if there is reorganization that recognizes the need which has been stated in the white paper where, on the first page, it refers to "new tactical and strategic concepts".
Make all our army units airborne units, and young men to whom the appeal is made will know that they are taking part in the most modern force that is in training anywhere. We do not need to look to any other country to devise the most effective use of manpower for the kind of force that will be needed for Canada. This statement applies to the militia as well as to the permanent force. Nor need this involve enormous expense in the first instance. Special transport aircraft would be required for the permanent force; but so far as militia units are concerned, these mock-ups of transport aircraft, made simply by joining the frame to the body of the aircraft, would be adequate for the purpose of giving training of that kind. Then selected units could be given training in regular transport aircraft of the type required.
I submit that, having regard to the imagination, having regard to the new concept required, as stated by the minister, what he has said to us today and what is said in the white paper is not only noncommittal but is extremely uninformative from the point of view of what we may hope for in the future.
We are still going to require conventional units in the Canadian army. We need conventional units, used in an unconventional way. With all earnestness I urge the minister to contemplate the possibility of giving immediate instructions to organize the army completely so that this huge country, with its 15 million people, may have the kind of hard-hitting, mobile airborne army units which could be put down at any point in Canada to meet whatever demands might be imposed upon them.
Then the question arises as to what the situation would be as a member of NATO. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that our most effective contribution to NATO will be to have the kind of combined force that is most effective for Canada. We are building an air force, not yet on the proportionate basis that would seem to be required for the

Supply-National Defence special position Canada occupies. But we have an air force of which every Canadian can be proud. I do want to say that twice in the last two years I have seen our squadrons overseas, and I can testify to what the minister has already said about their high standing among the squadrons now in Europe.
At Zweibrucken last summer I saw Canadian squadrons that were not only equal to but I think a little better than any other service squadrons in Europe at that time. It is unquestionably true that the new Sabre V jet with the Orenda engine, which gives that Sabre a higher speed than its corresponding United States counterpart, has not only given our squadrons an enviable reputation over there but has also given a very high morale to all the members of our air units in Europe at this time.
Nevertheless, the situation is changing rapidly over there. Germany's entry into NATO is soon going to change our requirements. It was essential that Canada should take its part in sending air and army units to Europe during the period Germany was disarmed completely and while there were uncertainties as to the course Germany might follow. Certainly, at a time when Russia was seeking to win Western Germany over to her point of view, it was essential that the people of West Germany be offered positive evidence that the nations united in NATO were joined in their determination to protect the soil of Western Germany from Russian invasion.
However, it will not be long before Western Germany will be rearmed to such an extent that she will be able to assume full responsibility for her own territory. In fact, Chancellor Konrad Adenauer only last Saturday stated in Bonn, just before his departure for Washington, that one of the three main objectives of the German government is to reach a point where it will be possible for the United States forces to withdraw from Germany. Obviously when he spoke of the United States forces he also had in mind the forces of Great Britain, France and Canada as well. Therefore our plans should be made with the knowledge that not only the army brigade now in Germany but also the air force units now in Germany may in the not too distant future be withdrawn.
Whether they are or not, the fact remains that stage by stage the need for Canadian army units in the protracted period of unsettled peace before us which, please God, may merge into a period of stable peace, is going to require fewer and fewer units from the North American continent. We therefore

can begin now to plan the type of units that would be needed. What, then, of our obligations to NATO?
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that if we organized here in Canada a unique Canadian army set-up of small, hard-hitting, compact units, able to move with the utmost speed to any threatened point, we would not only be devising the kind of unit best suited to meet any threat to this huge land area of ours, but we would also be devising the best type of force needed in the years ahead.
I am one of those who find a great source of confidence in the extent of the mutual danger which now threatens the nations on both sides. The extent of the destruction that would come from any thermonuclear war in itself offers the greatest possibility of avoiding a general world conflagration in which the main antagonists would be Russia on the one hand and the western nations on the other. We all recall the typically imaginative words of Sir Winston Churchill only a few months ago when he placed before the House of Commons in Great Britain all the menace of thermonuclear destruction, and then said, "By a strange anomaly it may appear that peace is the sturdy child of terror." That is a possibility.
After all, we have certain things in common with Russia. One of these is the desire to live. Not long ago in New York I saw in a great photographic exhibition there a picture of a Russian family gathered around a table, and at the end of the table there was a picture of a young man in uniform with a black border around the frame. There in an exhibition that had photographs from all over the world I could not help thinking that there were similar photographs from France, from Germany, from Italy, from the United States and from Canada.
We all like to think of our young people growing up and living normal lives. Whether they may place the same value on life as we do is only a comparative question. The Russians want to live and they want their children to live. The mere knowledge that their precipitation of a thermonuclear war would mean devastation of their own country and the death of their own children will be a deterrent even to the most terrible dictator in the Kremlin. For that reason I share the opinion of those who see great hope of the avoidance of another world war in the very fact that there is this terrible fear of destruction which could in fact end human life on this globe.
That does not end the possibility of war. At the time the war broke out in Korea all the terrible, destructive power of the atomic bomb was already available. At the time the

Russian-supported attacks in Indo-China were being carried on by the Viet Minh forces there were atomic bombs, as there were atomic bombs while there was fighting in Malaya, in Kenya and elsewhere throughout the world. The existence of these terrifying weapons has not stopped fighting with conventional weapons in Gaza; nor has it stopped fighting in other isolated areas in other parts of the world. Nevertheless it would appear that there are those who think they can afford the privilege of a war of their own without the danger of precipitating the use of those terrible weapons.
Let us hope that up to a point this is true. Whatever any of us may think about the decision not to bomb the Chinese bases from which the Chinese air force was attacking the troops of the United Nations in Korea, let us be quite sure of one thing. The fact that they were not bombed has undoubtedly encouraged the thought that it is possible to wage conventional war without inviting retaliation by these terrible weapons. For that reason there must be conventional units, and we must have our own type of conventional units for the future.
Therefore the thing for us to do to the best of our ability is devise the kind of force that would meet not only our own requirements but could play its part as one of the members of the United Nations in an outbreak of that kind. How best can Canada be a partner in dealing with one of these conflagrations? Will it be by the slow movement by rail and ship of old-fashioned army units or by the sudden movement, perhaps within 48 or 72 hours, to Asia or Africa or Indo-China of the kind of hard-hitting mobile units we have been suggesting? I am satisfied that when it came to a discussion of Canada's participation, if we said we were concentrating on army units of that type and that we would assume our responsibility within the NATO organization by the movement of units of that type, they would welcome the possibility and possibly other countries might themselves follow the same course.
The picture before us is by no manner of means dark and hopeless. There are great reasons for hope. There are reasons for hope that under the overhanging threat of mutual destruction the largest nations may not precipitate the kind of war that would make that kind of destruction a reality. Perhaps we may be moving closer than we think to the very time when the threat they face will impose some measure of sanity and frankness and honesty upon the representatives of communist Russia. Perhaps the very fact that they realize the danger to their own homeland will give us some reason to hope that
Supply-National Defence beyond the doubtful gestures we have already seen will be real gestures toward mutual disarmament which will end this mad race which is costing Canada over $2 billion a year, and which is imposing such heavy burdens upon the whole world. In the meantime let us be sure not only that we have the most economical force but that we also have the most efficient force for our own requirements.
I regret that the minister has made no positive statement which would offer a new understanding of the intentions of the department. They have had such a statement in Great Britain. When the white paper was placed before the members of parliament in Britain a very dramatic statement was made with far-reaching significance. It was said there that they have decided definitely that battleships are now primarily launching bases for guided missiles. That revolutionizes the movement of naval forces. I want to take this opportunity to address a few remarks to the committee, particularly on the question of defence research. Before I continue I want to congratulate our Minister of National Defence. I feel that he has achieved a fine grasp of the details of his department; and as we have seen, he is ready to take prompt executive action whenever he feels the need for it arises.
A further point I want to mention is that as associate minister of national defence and also since he has become Minister of National Defence he has always shown a conscientious and considerate interest in members of parliament in respect of the arrangements he makes for our visits to defence establishments. I am sure these visits have broadened the knowledge of members with regard to defence to a considerable degree.
Looking at the figure in the estimates we see that there is a total of some $1,769 million appropriated for defence generally. Of this a sum of $52 J million, in round figures, is set aside for the defence research board. The latter figure represents almost exactly 2-9 per cent of the total figure to be budgeted for in respect of defence expenditure. Although we in this country are, of course, still extremely vulnerable to enemy attack, international tensions have eased to a certain extent, and perhaps it might be an appropriate time to examine the money spent on research in relation to total defence expenditure, taking a realistic view.
We have here a country with a very large land mass but comparatively thinly populated, backed by a more than adequate storehouse of natural resources. Although we can contribute our fair share to any joint defence effort by the free nations, we cannot obviously supply sufficiently large armies, navies and air forces to undertake continental defence on a large scale independently of the other countries, involving huge areas of land and for a long period of time. Perhaps our most effective contribution to defence would be to specialize in some particular field, and this course has been suggested by many of those hon. members who have spoken in this debate today.
Whatever we may conclude in that respect -and one is tempted to conclude that we certainly could look twice at specializing in air power-we can arrive at this conclusion. There is one field to which we are perfectly suited in this country, and that is the field of research as applied to our defence effort.
I am more particularly interested in two fields, namely atomic fission and electronics. As to the first, the field of atomic energy and atomic fission, presumably most of our research is carried on by Atomic Energy of
4894	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence Canada Limited, operating at Chalk River under a budget of some $18 million. This program is carried on under the aegis of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I thought perhaps we might consider a parallel program carried on under the Department of National Defence to study a different though related field. For example, we do not appear to have done much, if any, work in the field of propulsion of vehicles, both on land and on sea, by atomic energy. The United States has had some experience in this field. We know they have constructed a submarine powered by an atomic engine and have another one under construction. We also know they are contemplating the construction of a freighter to be propelled by atomic energy.
It would seem from the white paper that our research is limited to a study of the effects of thermonuclear explosion, and it would not appear that we have undertaken any separate or distinct attack on this field by way of atomic research other than studying the effect of the explosion of atomic and hydrogen bombs. Perhaps we should broaden our base. If we could achieve success in the field of propulsion of vehicles by atomic energy, certainly the effect on our defence forces would be very salutary indeed, and would give us a tremendous advantage in so far as other countries are concerned.
Let us look at the field of electronics. In this respect the white paper indicates on page 37 that the defence research board's program of grants in aid at Canadian universities continues at a scale that has levelled off at $1 million annually. Again, on page 38 the white paper indicates that the board's support of physical electronics research at universities continues. In other words, it would appear that electronics research is confined to work at universities supported by grants in aid totalling $1 million annually. The white paper goes on to say that a comparatively small scientific staff at the defence research telecommunications establishment is doing research in special fields, particularly with regard to the application of electronics to the mid-Canada radar warning system.
From a casual perusal of the estimates and the white paper it would appear to me that the sum of $1 million annually devoted to this wide and complicated field of electronics research as applied to defence measures is quite inadequate to press forward the advance of pure knowledge. I would suggest that the minister give some consideration to that situation.
Of the $52 million appropriated for research, $28 million is for the construction of buildings and the acquisition of equipment. Apparently


this will provide the necessary space in which people may work. It does not look as though that would be a continuing expenditure on research. The money is to provide space where people can work and will not necessarily be applied to the actual work of research. The money actually going into the work of research would therefore be somewhat less than the $52 million indicated in the estimates. We must take this into consideration.
Looking at the comparison between expenditures on research and total defence expenditures we should also consider one further point. Money spent on research brings a double reward. On the one hand it contributes to the security of the country by assisting the fighting forces. On the other hand it provides knowledge which, when made public-and it is made public-creates opportunities in civilian fields of endeavour. Thus, while on the one hand providing security and hence the opportunity to go on living, through research you also bring about a situation whereby further opportunities are created, resulting in the long run in paying the dividend of increasing the standard of living. That is extremely important.
A concrete example of this sort of thing was made apparent on our visit to Fort Churchill. We were shown the research work that had been done by the branch of the defence research board there. Investigations had been made into conditions of life in an Arctic environment. Types of clothing were devised. Methods of constructing buildings with a permafrost foundation were worked out. Investigations were made into the type of food one should eat and how to heat buildings. All this material was the work of the defence research board at Fort Churchill.
On the other hand, when private companies go up there for the purpose of constructing such installations as the D.E.W. line, all the material collected through careful research by the federal government is available free of charge, I was told, to these private companies in order that they may carry out their work to the best advantage. Therefore the research undertaken provides information for private civilian organizations, and we reap a double reward from the money spent. I think that is an extremely important point. It is a chance to more or less have our cake and eat it too, something we do not encounter too often.
I therefore submit respectfully that at this time we can afford to perhaps change the emphasis on our defence planning to the point where more money will be channelled into the vital field of research. My submission, and I ask the minister to consider it, is that

if the money spent on research were tripled, increased to say $150 million, it would not involve too great a departure from accepted principles. It would not impair the present defence effort; it would give impetus and breadth to our research program, and it would still amount to less than 10 per cent of total defence expenditures.
