Mr. Chairman, in the white paper issued by the minister's department there are set out on page 3 the objectives of Canada's defence program. I presume they are set out there in order of importance, and if I am incorrect in that assumption I know the minister will correct me. First is the defence of Canada; second is co-operation with the United States in the joint defence of Canada and the United States; third, cooperation within the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, looking toward the checking of aggression; and, fourth, the carrying out of undertakings by Canada as a member of the United Nations. Bearing those in mind as the general defence objectives of Canada, I should like to relate my remarks for the next few minutes to the defence objectives of Canada with particular relation to the navy.
It will be recalled that in the days of world war II the emphasis with regard to the work of the navy was on escort and convoy work, and hon. members know that in that war the Canadian navy did the great bulk of escort duty in the north Atlantic. Since world war II it has become rather apparent that the objectives and purposes of the naval program have been directed along these same lines, and unless I am badly mistaken it would appear that the emphasis is still largely on this objective, namely escort work. I would refer hon. members to page 15 of the white paper, paragraph 47, which reads:
In January, 1952, for the protection of vital sea communications between Europe and North America, a supreme allied commander, Atlantic (SACLANT), was appointed and headquarters established at Norfolk, Va.

That particular item refers to part 3, Canada's role in defence abroad. I gathered from the minister's remarks this morning that the work of the Canadian navy was largely anti-submarine work in particular relationship to escort duty. Another objective of Canadian navy policy has been the defence of Canadian waters and harbours. While this has been an important aspect of the work of the navy in the past, I think somewhat less emphasis has been placed upon this aspect of naval work more recently. My feeling is that at the present time this is in a somewhat secondary position to the escort and convoy work.
Due to modern and changing conditions since world war II I think the emphasis on the work of the navy should be re-examined. It was pointed out this morning by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich that conditions in the world have greatly changed, and that our whole policy could quite properly be re-examined. My view is that emphasis should be placed upon the defence of Canadian waters, Canadian harbours and Canadian inland cities. This may seem a rather strange job for the navy to be doing, that is protecting Canadian inland cities and the industrial heartland of Canada, but I shall elaborate on this a little more in the next few moments.
On page 4 of the white paper and also in his remarks this morning the minister has brought home most forcefully the danger of nuclear war, and there is the plain statement that if such an event takes place there is no real defence against it, that the only thing we can hope to do is minimize the results of such an attack. I think there is little doubt in the minds of most people that if war of this type takes place it will occur very suddenly and unexpectedly.
A great deal of emphasis has been placed in the last few years, particularly this year, on the danger of an attack on North America by aircraft coming in over the north pole or from the north Atlantic or from the Pacific. In view of this the "Pinetree" and mid-Canada defence lines, and now the D.E.W. line, have been set up as radar warning systems to warn the industrial heartland of Canada and the United States of the approach of enemy aircraft.
While these are extremely important, we all know there is another way by which aircraft and missiles could be directed at the industrial heart of North America. This would be quite apart from direct attacks by any enemy craft based in Europe or Asia. I refer to the possibility of the launching of guided missiles or even small jet aircraft from
Supply

National Defence submarines. I do not thing there is any argument that this possibility is great; but because of the emphasis placed upon possible attacks by aircraft from bases in Europe or Asia it is possible that this matter has been overlooked or has not been emphasized as much as it should be.

Mr. Chairman, prior to the recess I pointed out that, in the work of the Royal Canadian Navy, I believe the emphasis should be shifted from escort work to defence of our home waters, for reasons I shall outline in the next few moments.
I agree with the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich that, because of changes in the world military situation owing to nuclear weapons and other advances, our whole defence concept ought to be changed. I also agree with the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich that the only effective enemy attack on Canada or on the United States or both would be made by air. But at present all the emphasis is on the fact that this attack might be made by land-based aircraft coming from either Europe or Asia.
We have, of course, the three radar defence lines that have been much discussed in the last day or so, but attacks by air can also come from other sources than land-based aircraft in Europe or Asia. By that I mean there is a fairly strong possibility-indeed a probability-that an attack could be made on
4900	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence industry in the heartland of North America by either guided missiles or jet planes launched from submarines.
We have been accustomed to thinking, for example, of Hudson bay and James bay as a large, cold, inland sea belonging to Canada, and a very innocuous place; but I should like to point out that I believe Hudson bay and James bay could very well be the dagger pointed at the heart of Canada and North America generally. We have had samples of things such as this in the past. I think every hon. member here well remembers that England built a mighty fortress at Singapore. They were sure an attack would be made by the Japanese fleet. Great guns 18 inches in diameter were set up to repulse any such attack. As nearly everyone remembers, the Japanese captured Singapore, but they never used their navy. They used small numbers of troops landed behind, where nobody thought any attack would come from.
We may have a D.E.W. line, a mid-Canada defence line and a "Pinetree" line to warn us of attack by land-based aircraft, but I do not think sufficient emphasis has been placed on the possibility of attacks being made on our heartland by submarine-based aircraft or guided missiles coming from submarines that could easily invade certain strategic waters around Canada.
First I mention Hudson bay, just as a matter of interest. The distances I shall give are only approximations. They may be a mile or two out one way or the other. I also mention a submarine in James bay launching guided missiles or aircraft. I also put in a further qualification. While we have heard of guided missiles that may be able to travel from one continent to another, I am assuming that guided missiles can travel only from 300 to 500 miles. I have no doubt they can travel much farther, but I am basing my assumption on the smaller guided missiles and from experience of the last war.
We know that guided missiles undoubtedly exist. If they were launched from a submarine in Hudson bay they could certainly hit important areas in Canada. I would point out that the cities of Port Arthur and Fort William are only approximately 350 air miles from James bay. The Sault Ste. Marie canal area is only 300 miles away. Sudbury, with its great nickel mines and refinery, is only 300 miles away, and Ottawa about 400. The great dam at Des Joachims, up the Ottawa river, which furnishes the power for a great deal of the industrial area of Ontario, is about 400 miles distant. Montreal is 450 miles away, and the Toronto, Hamilton, Niagara area is approximately 500 miles away, or slightly better. The new St. Lawrence seaway will be 

about 400 miles away. I think these thoughts are at least worthy of note, and to my mind and the minds of other people with whom I have discussed the matter they are disturbing.
Another body of water from which attacks of this type could be made is the gulf of Maine. I know full well that the defence of the waters of the gulf of Maine is primarily the responsibility of the United States government, but because Canada could be affected too I feel that we also have responsibilities. Some of the air distances from the gulf of Maine to central Canada are not too great. Montreal is about 300 miles away, the seaway project about 300 miles away, Ottawa about 350 and the Toronto, Hamilton, Niagara area about 450 miles away.
I have often heard people say that if submarines were to get into the gulf of St. Lawrence they might, by attacks such as I have already outlined, cause a great deal of destruction. That is no doubt true of certain areas, but I think the Hudson bay and gulf of Maine areas are much more likely because they are closer. The gulf of St. Lawrence is about 400 miles away from Montreal and about 300 miles away from Quebec and Arvida with its aluminum plant. There are also other areas in Canada that could be attacked which are very obvious. In the east there are the cities of Halifax, Saint John and Moncton and on the west coast there are Vancouver and Kitimat, though I understand the Kitimat project is supposed to be proof against attacks such as these.
Another interesting fact is that the radium mines at Great Bear lake are only about 300 miles from the Arctic ocean. In certain months of the summer the Arctic ocean north of Canada is ice free and quite navigable by submarine. In these strategic waters, and I refer particularly to Hudson bay and the gulf of St. Lawrence, there are narrow entrances. Hudson strait, the entrance to Hudson bay, is about 100 miles wide. While the strait is about 400 miles long, it could well be defended. The distance across Cabot strait and the gulf of St. Lawrence is somewhat less than 100 miles. Of course the gulf of St. Lawrence can be entered by way of the strait of Belle Isle, but it is very narrow and would not present too much difficulty from the point of view of defence.
I have already mentioned the coastal waters off the maritime provinces, Labrador, the gulf of Maine, and the west coast. The question arises, can we defend these areas adequately at the present time? With respect, Mr. Chairman, I think not. In order to guard these coastal waters against sneak attacks by submarines I think some type of patrol would have to be established. When I think of

patrols first of all I refer to the navy and its ships, but one has also to think of air patrols.
To deal first with ships, with our present and contemplated navy I think it would be very difficult to patrol all these areas adequately with our own ships or even with ships which no doubt would be available to us from the United States. On page 5 of the white paper I notice a reference to home defence and Canada-United States co-operation. Certainly nothing specific is mentioned about joint operations between Canadian and American ships for this purpose, although I am sure it must be in mind and ships are probably available for this type of work.
On page 7 of the white paper I see that at the present time we have in commission ten destroyer escort ships, one undergoing conversion and 14 under construction. Those under construction are of course the new St. Laurent class, the first of which I understand is to go into commission probably late this year. That will eventually make a total of 25.
There are also a number of frigates in commission, though there seems to be a slight discrepancy as to the actual number. On page 7 of the white paper it is set out that there are nine in commission with eleven in reserve and one undergoing conversion, but on page 41 it says that there are ten in commission. I dare say this minor discrepancy can be explained. In any event, the fact is that we have very few ships in commission, held in reserve or under construction to deal with the very large area to be covered.
In addition, certain areas from which submarines might launch attacks, such as the bay of Fundy and the gulf of St. Lawrence, are difficult areas for technical reasons from the point of view of anti-submarine protection. There are currents in the waters and temperature changes that cause some difficulties in certain types of detecting equipment. At least they did in the last war and immediately afterward. These difficulties may have been overcome, but if they have no doubt it is secret and of course could not be told.
Regarding patrols by aircraft, as every hon. member knows weather conditions necessarily limit the type of patrol work that can be done adequately by aircraft. It is true that we have aircraft equipped with radar and other devices, and that in very bad weather patrol work can be done by helicopters and other types of reconnaissance planes such as the new Neptune to be used by the air force, which I had the pleasure of seeing at a distance recently, but despite this the
Supply-National Defence major proportion of the work of patrolling strategic waters will have to be done by ships of some sort.
There are of course other dangers. There is what I consider the relatively minor danger of mine-laying in certain waters by enemy submarine. However, I see we have eight new minesweepers and six more under construction. No doubt these may be adequate for the purpose for the immediate future. I was very glad to note in the minister's comments earlier today that the Royal Navy had lent us two submarines to carry on antisubmarine detection exercises. I am glad to hear this because it is certainly difficult for crews in training to know how to operate their instruments if they do not have the real thing to work on.
However, I have one reservation. I rather imagine the submarines that have been lent us for this purpose by the Royal Navy are not of the newest variety. They are probably somewhat ancient, and not the type of submarine the Canadian navy would be compelled to deal with in the event of an attack. Undoubtedly the submarines Russia or any other potential enemy might have would be much larger and speedier. While exercises in detection using what I imagine are older types of submarine are better than nothing at all, they are necessarily limited by that fact.
I should also like to touch briefly on the question of manpower and recruiting. On page 22 of the white paper we see in the first paragraph that the maximum strength for the navy is 20,000. At present, as the minister informed us, and as I also learned from the answer to a question that recently appeared on the order paper, there are approximately 19,000 men in the Royal Canadian Navy. The question arises in my mind, in what way is the figure of 20,000 men related to the ships and equipment planned at present and to be completed within the next few years? That seems to me rather vague. Are these 20,000 men designed to equip the ships and shore establishments we have at the moment, or are they designed to equip the ships we will have within the next three or four years when the new St. Laurent class destroyers are added.
I might point out when these 14 new destroyers are added they will have approximately 270 to 300 men each. Is this figure of 20,000 men also related to these frigates which are held in reserve or in dehumidification, I think the term is in the white paper? As I recall it, frigates formerly had a complement of 150 to 160 men. No doubt with all the improvements more will be required. If 10 or 11 of these are to be kept in reserve,

Supply-National Defence are they to be manned? Will there be adequate personnel available to man these ships included in the 20,000 figure? Those are questions about which I am curious, and I should like to have an answer from the minister later.
I come now to the question of recruiting and recruiting costs. I notice that again these costs are related to this figure of 20,000. I see that the estimates for recruiting costs are slightly less this year than last. As hon. members know, each year a certain number of men leave the navy for one reason or another. At this point I should like to refer to some figures contained in an answer to a question put on the order paper on February 28 last by the hon. member for Calgary North. According to this answer the naval strength on December 31, 1954 was 18,806. Enrolments during 1954 were 4,703 and releases were 2,262, making a net gain of 2,441 men. This would appear to be quite satisfactory.
The costs of recruiting were also shown in the answer to this question placed on the order paper by the hon. member for Calgary North. The cost of recruiting for the navy last year was $943,300. This amounts to approximately $200 per man, but I think this is a rather misleading figure and illustrates the story about the statistician six feet tall who drowned in a river whose average depth was four feet.
These figures can be misleading, because I suggest that a large number, perhaps more than half, of the men who enlisted in the navy would have enlisted without any costly advertising. This figure probably includes the cost of recruiting centres and so on, which are constant costs. I am considering such things as advertising costs and teams going around recruiting people. A large number of the recruits probably would have entered the navy without any of that. Actually the high cost of recruiting is related to the amount expended for the last 30 or 40 per cent of the recruits you get each year.
So far as the actual costs of advertising are concerned, the total cost last year was $290,000. This works out to about $60 per man, based on 1954 enlistments. Again I suggest this is misleading, as a large percentage of these people would have entered the service anyway. The advertising costs per man are probably related to the last 30 or 40 per cent of your recruits. The cost per man, therefore, would probably be closer to $125.
My suggestion is that a lot of the advertising in the newspapers might very well be cut out. It is very expensive, and I think it can be done by other methods. A great many people do wish to join the navy. It is a very [Mr. Nesbitt.1

fine service, as some of us know personally and others know by repute. People who wish to join can obtain information from the numerous divisional headquarters which are scattered around the country.
I think the best type of advertising for the navy is the type of advertising illustrated not very long ago in the city of Peterborough. The hon. member for Peterborough may wish to make some further remarks about this, so I hope he will pardon me for bringing it up at the moment. The naval veterans' association held a meeting in Peterborough. There were over 2,000 naval veterans present, representing nine of the ten provinces of Canada. There was a very fine program for two days, to which a great deal of free newspaper publicity was given. The event was talked about by everybody, and it was very successful.
I feel this is one of the best types of advertising. Instead of spending a lot of money on newspaper advertising which, like election advertisements, a great many people do not read at all, the money might very well be spread out over some of these naval veterans' associations for Sunday church parades, financing naval bands and that sort of thing. Everybody likes a parade; and while I would probably receive some challenge on this, I believe the naval service and the naval veterans certainly march as well as any of the other services. I believe that from the point of view of the naval bands it would be good for their morale to get a chance to go around and play for the public more than they do. I think this is a more effective type of publicity than any newspaper advertising, and more recruits might well be gained.
Another thing that might well be considered are these travelling teams who go around trying to get recruits for the navy. I see that last year the cost of these travelling teams amounted to $138,091, and other costs of recruiting for the navy amounted to $499,683. Apparently some of these amounts were joint costs which had to be shared with the army and air force recruiting teams. It seems to me that while we might run into objection in some quarters, some of these recruiting teams explain the advantages of naval and other service life to students and those in industrial plants. It should be a good way of getting the first-class recruits who are necessary to maintain the present high standard of the naval service.
There is another suggestion I should like to make in this regard. It concerns the number of people who are expected to come into the navy, who belong to the university naval training division. There are a great

many students who take this university naval training who get summer cruises and have a pleasant time. This is a good way to absorb the atmosphere of the navy and no doubt acquire a certain amount of valuable training. Perhaps I have been misinformed on this and if I have I am sure the minister will correct me, but I wonder if those summer cruises could be confined to those who intend to make a career of the navy rather than include those who might be going along for the ride, so to speak.
The last item upon which I should like to touch very briefly is this matter of naval research, referred to on page 39 of the white paper. This is the part of the white paper which deals with defence research generally, and there is one very small paragraph touching on naval research. No doubt some of the other types of research will directly affect the navy, but this small paragraph indicates there is very little research being conducted directly for the navy.
I see according to a newspaper dispatch that the new St. Laurent class of destroyer escorts are costing about $15 million each.
I am not suggesting we are not getting value for what is being paid out. So far as destroyers are concerned the cost of the prototype or first destroyer in the class is great because many alterations have to be made.
But it would be a pretty sad thing, after building ships costing that much money and manned by about 300 men, to lose such ships and men. It would be a heavy loss of men and material. It seems to me naval research might very well be directed to finding out if there is not some less expensive but equally effective device for detecting submarines in the strategic waters surrounding the Canadian coast, particularly those I mentioned earlier in my speech.
Possibly this would involve some small vessel which could carry adequate detecting equipment, but which would not be expected to destroy enemy submarines. Larger ships or aircraft could be used for that purpose. Possibly use could be made of modified or advanced types of detection cables. Hon. members know these were used in the last war to protect the harbours. These could be used to good effect, it seems to me, at the entrances to such waters as Hudson bay or Cabot strait.
Canada is not a country that can afford much higher defence costs. If naval research could find approved methods of protecting ourselves, without greatly increasing the cost, it seems to me something that would be desirable. We all know the extent to which the income tax dollar is eaten up for defence
Supply-National Defence purposes. For this reason I am not advocating greatly increased expenditures, unless they are absolutely necessary. It seems to me a substitute method of protecting our waters might very well be found through increased naval research.

Mr. Chairman, it is not easy to discuss matters of defence at a time in the history of warfare when things are changing as rapidly as they have in the last few years. Modern scientific inventions, new types of weapons and the growing effectiveness of air power are making it very difficult for those in charge of defence matters to keep abreast of developments. The minister is aware of that fact, of course, and his advisers know it only too well.
Nevertheless I thought in the course of the minister's statement earlier today he showed some lack of imagination with regard to the present state of affairs. It was a cautious statement; perhaps it had to be. On the other hand I thought the problem might have been approached a little more vigorously. The minister has had two years of experience in the department. Before becoming minister he was associate minister for a year, so he is not unfamiliar with the task. What struck me was that too much of what he had to say closely resembled what was said by the previous minister the year before.
Incidentally, unless I heard the minister incorrectly, I thought he was out a bit in his history when he was talking about the importance of defence in Canada. I understood him to say that for a century and a half there had been no fighting on Canadian soil. If he said that, I hope he will not object to my reminding him that there was considerable fighting on Canadian soil between 1812 and 1814. Then there was some fighting in 1837 and 1838, with rather serious casualties among the forces involved. The Fenian raids of 1866 and 1870 caused great disturbance among people engaged in defence in Canada, and rather serious casualties were suffered. As many as from 10,000 to 20,000 militiamen were called out and put under arms for varying periods of time during those troubles. So we have not been altogether free from disturbances on Canadian soil.
I have noticed, in reading the history of that period, that the problem of defending Canada loomed as large to the men of that day as the present problem does to us. For those who are interested I would recommend a book by a most competent historian, "Canada's Soldiers, 1604 to 1954", which

Supply-National Defence
gives the picture of the early days in Canada's defence. This book is written by Professor Stanley of the Royal Military College at Kingston.
A hundred years ago people examining the problem of defending Canada estimated that because of the size of the country-and it was much smaller to them than it is to us-and the long border between Canada and the United States, 150,000 men would be needed effectively to man our defences. So the problem has been a pressing one throughout the greater part of Canada's history. It is only since our relationship with the United States has become very friendly that we have been able to ignore the southern border.
Other members speaking in the debate have pointed out how our thinking has changed to the point where we are now stressing a more complete defence of the North American continent, which is open to attack both by air and by sea. As the hon. member for Oxford pointed out a few moments ago, even in the Hudson bay area submarines might launch missiles against our cities or other places.
So we have to take a new look at Canada's defences. For several years members of the official opposition have been advocating greater mobility of Canada's forces. This applies at the present time, when you are thinking only of the Canadian scene. And it is here I believe the minister lacked imagination. Several members who have spoken have drawn attention to the possibility of air attack and the means that should be taken to meet such attack. For several years we have had a mobile striking force which from time to time has been exercised in part in its peculiar role. But I do not think it is a complete mobile attacking force. I believe it needs other arms added to it. In addition to infantry, artillery, and engineers which are now dropped by parachute, along with their artillery and other weapons and supplies, I wonder if thought has been given to carrying by air small tanks to assist a force which had to land and dislodge an enemy. The minister has not dealt with that. I do not know whether the glider has passed out of use, or whether it has been developed beyond the excellent stage it reached during the second world war. Helicopters, for carrying supplies to forces, have come within the ken of the defence department, because I see that some have been purchased and are going to be used on these northern radar lines for carrying supplies. So perhaps experience will be obtained there.

Considerable mention has been made of the radar warning lines now under construction. The minister has drawn our attention to the fact that dependence is being placed on the interceptor planes of the air force, rather than on ground-to-air missiles which, I judge from what I have been reading, have not reached that stage of development where they could be safely relied upon in time of emergency. I find that many United States cities are ringed with batteries of these ground-to-air missiles, which prompted a competent observer to say that it is the last defence weapon. The range is limited, and the attacking bomber might be destroyed too close to the populated area to afford any effective defence.
In considering the defence of Canada along those lines, I think we would find more satisfaction here had the minister given us a better picture of the defence of Canada. As far as I can remember, the situation is exactly the same as it was several years ago. We are to have a mobile striking force with an increased number of planes. We are now placing our dependence on the radar warning lines. Last year, when we heard about the one that was in existence, we made some inquiries of the former minister of defence in regard to the effectiveness of that warning line. Now we are to have three. I do not recall that the present minister was overly confident as to the value of radar defence lines.
That is the great problem. No sooner are these things constructed and put into operation than they become obsolete. The same thing applies to the planes and the guided missiles that are developed. However, in addition to considering the defence of Canada along those lines we have other commitments. Our commitment overseas with NATO involves the use of conventional weapons. We also shall not be free from responsibility,
I suppose, if some war breaks out after the fashion of Korea, in which case the United Nations would expect member nations to participate. Despite the fact that we are living in this atomic era, conventional weapons may be required in conflicts of that nature.
The minister has indicated to us that the formation of the defence force is still just about what it was a year ago, two years ago, three years ago. The hon. member for Esqui-malt-Saanich has pointed out that it is largely an infantry force that has been provided. During the time I have been in the House of Commons I have done everything in my power to urge that armour be given more prominence in the Canadian army, so long as we have to prepare to use an army such

as we know now and have known in the past. My remarks along that line were not received very acceptably by the present minister's predecessor; but I hoped we would have a new look at the problem with a new man on the job. Imagine my disappointment to find that in the minister's statement describing our present forces he devoted one sentence to mentioning that we had two armoured regiments, and that was it. In the white paper I do not find much mention of armour except under the heading of militia, so there we are.
The great demand of modern times in the type of force that is in Europe is mobility, and you get mobility from armoured vehicles and from tracked vehicles, which can go across country. I hope ten years after the second world war we are not still depending on wheeled vehicles tied to the road for the forces in Europe. But I judge that the Canadian brigade is. Wheeled vehicles tied to the road extend for such an immense distance, are so easily blocked and pile up so easily behind one another that it is very hard to keep an army supplied. Modern thinking on forces such as we have in Europe is that supplying should be done by way of helicopter or some type of plane that can leap over and drop those supplies, or land with them in the area where they are most needed, rather than get them only from the wheeled vehicle in the supply column.
Of course I have time and again suggested that supplies, particularly of ammunition and petrol, might well be taken forward in a tracked vehicle which would have crosscountry performance. Despite this emphasis on armour; despite the fact that leading generals continue to comment on the need for mobility, as General Montgomery did last year-and I have an article here by General Gale also emphasizing the same point -the Canadian army is out of balance with regard to armour. The armoured corps, which was of such great importance in the second world war, and continues or should continue to be of great importance at this time, is suffering from neglect in the Canadian army.
I notice that in the tests carried out in Nevada, upon which the minister did not dwell, armour including tanks and armoured personnel carriers were used much closer to ground zero than the infantry troops who were sheltering in trenches. Those armoured vehicles were just 12,000 feet away from ground zero, if the diagram in the Globe and
Supply-National Defence Mail of April 25 is correct. In the report of that experiment in the same paper I find this statement:
On the military side, there was staged the first atomic-explosion exercise by an armoured task force. It involved 450 men, 57 tanks and 24 armoured personnel carriers.
The task force executed an 8-mile breakthrough manoeuvre in an hour immediately after the detonation.
This indicates, Mr. Chairman, that armour has a place even on the battlefield where atomic weapons have been exploded, and that it will provide safety for the gunners, the drivers and the infantry in those vehicles.
In view of the continued importance of armour, I cannot understand why the Department of National Defence neglects it in the Canadian army. I am not going to repeat the arguments I used last year, but to my mind they are the most effective of all. One of the arguments I used last year was that unless we build up the armoured corps within the Canadian army, and train the high command in the use of armour, we shall pay a very severe penalty sometime in the future if we are compelled to engage in war; for as I said last year, the training of the high command is of greater importance, in my own experience, than almost anything else.
I notice we are informed in the white paper that the tank is to play the anti-tank role, and in the militia the artillery is being accordingly reduced. If that is being done in the militia why is it not being done in the regular army? There is no mention of that in the white paper.
The tank is considered by the Canadian army to be a difficult offensive weapon against which infantry may have to defend themselves, and a new type of infantry anti-tank weapon has been designed under Canadian direction. Credit is due to those who have effected that improvement. It is an improved version of the Piat or the Bazooka and is called the Heller, which indicates a surprising lack of vocabulary in naming a new weapon. But it is considered a much more effective anti-tank weapon for infantry than its predecessors.
I am always amazed when I see pictures of these anti-tank weapons in the hands of infantrymen. The infantryman is shown as either standing or kneeling. That is a good way to go underground permanently, to stand or kneel when using an anti-tank weapon if there are tanks in the vicinity. I think the public are confused by pictures of that nature. I believe with a little imagination the people who display weapons like that for the information of the public might show a picture of the weapon by itself, or show the men in a

Supply-National Defence trench with a bit of concealment or cover. Don't fool yourself; you can have an antitank weapon twice the size of the Heller, and if you stand or kneel to fire it, a little speculative firing from the machine guns on the oncoming tank will wipe out such infantrymen.
The defence department considers that the tank is still going to be used, because it has provided a weapon against it. It has indicated that it would use tanks against tanks, so the tank is not an obsolete or outmoded vehicle. Yet the defence department fails to give the importance to armour in the Canadian forces that it should. Other countries have built up their armoured forces and are continuing to emphasize their importance.
This brings me to a topic on which I have spoken frequently in this house, the armoured personnel carrier. I do not want to cover again ground that I have covered before, but I do want to ask the minister the same question I asked his predecessor. If you are going to fight with conventional weapons, if you are visualizing an army engaged on a battlefield as in the second world war; if the terrain over which the army is going to be engaged will permit the use of tanks, which means you are not fighting in a swamp or jungle, then we should provide armoured personnel carriers for the infantry. Do not repeat the experience of the first and second world wars by condemning infantrymen to walking across open ground to take up a position. I regret to^ say that I think that is the type of training still being given in the Canadian army.
I raised this question with the minister's predecessor on more than one occasion, and I always received the customary brush-off. The armoured personnel carrier was mentioned on page 39 of the white paper of last year, where it was stated that the army was developing a new tracked carrier for the infantry. I questioned whether that was really an armoured personnel carrier. In the white paper of this year, on page 42, they have come up with this statement:
In addition, the Canadian army is conducting trials on British and United States army types of armoured personnel carrier to determine their suitability to meet the needs of the Canadian army.
It is only ten years since the last war, and perhaps I am getting a bit impatient. The armoured personnel carrier was the product of Canadian ingenuity, and credit is generally given to General Simonds for conceiving the idea. It was developed by Canadians to a certain pitch of efficiency and it saved hundreds and hundreds of lives in the second world war. My plea is, can we not continue 
that type of training in the Canadian army? I had hoped that, with that experience, within this ten-year period Canada would have been foremost in the use of that particular vehicle.
It was not fully developed in the second world war. There were other ways of making use of the armoured personnel carrier. For the information of those who are not familiar with it may I say that in the second world war it consisted of the Ram tank, which was made in Canada, with the turret removed. The interior could then take a section of eight infantrymen with their weapons, and they could be carried from the concentration area to the assembly point, the starting line or right to the enemy's position without any casualties whatsoever. The proof was in the second world war.
I read many interesting stories of the second world war, and I wonder why with that type of vehicle available the high command has been a little slow in making use of it. There was a good story in the Legionary of March, 1955, dealing with an attack on the Hochwald forest. This particular battalion crossed 500 yards of open ground. It was a brilliant and courageous attack, but a very costly one because of heavy casualties involved. We were there; I know the ground, every inch of it. We were there with armoured personnel carriers and they were not used. Of course the reason was beyond my knowledge because I was not sitting in the seats of authority of the corps or the division or the army. But that is the type of story you read about the second world war and the first world war; gallant actions, but so wasteful of life.
I urge the Minister of National Defence to investigate again this problem of the armoured personnel carrier. The British are using them and so are the United States.
I do not know the particular types and they may not be effective, nevertheless they are using them. The United States used them at the recent exercise in Nevada with apparent success and I think we should have them.
The minister drew our attention to the great exercise last year in Germany, the "Battle Royal" it was called, at which our brigade acquitted itself admirably, as Canadian troops do on all occasions. He did not say whether they just walked on their flat feet as their predecessors did in the second world war, in the first world war and in the Boer war. Let us advance with the times.
The armoured personnel carrier can be used for battalion work; it can be used for company work; it can be used for a mopping-up action by a platoon. My contention is that the army should give close attention to this. I fear they have not done so, because

I read in the white paper that they are just investigating to see whether these United Kingdom or United States vehicles may be suitable for Canadian conditions.
I do not like to appear too critical of the service in which I spent quite a bit of my life, but I do draw attention to this lapse in the thinking of the Canadian army. We all know that it is important not to prepare for the next war on the basis of the last one and without any new ideas, but at the same time it is essential to draw from experience and make as effective a fighting force as you can with the knowledge you have.
I appreciate the immense problem there is in these times. The hydrogen bomb and the smaller atomic weapons seemed to change things so completely and make them very confusing. But it is not beyond the capabilities of our experienced army commanders to devise ways and means of coping with these new problems.
After all, when we are discussing national defence we are thinking of two or three things. We are thinking of the defence of our own country. We are thinking of cooperative defence under the NATO organization. We must think of how efficient our navy, army and air forces are, and we must think in terms of the men who man the ships and the airplanes and who serve in the artillery and the armoured formations of the infantry. We must think in terms of ensuring their effective training so they will be competent fighting men, and we must also think in terms of saving their lives by every possible known device.
It is only for that reason that I have taken the time of the committee to stress once again the importance of armour as protection for our fighting men.

Mr. Chairman, we have had today a considerable amount of discussion of many of the important aspects of defence. I do not wish to be repetitious; therefore I shall say little or nothing about many of these matters as to some of which I hope the minister will provide answers.
In the four years previous to this, Canada's defence objectives were stated in the same terms. They appear in last year's white paper -that for 1954-55-at page 6, and read in this way:
The objectives of our defence policy remain the same as heretofore:
(i)	the immediate defence of Canada and North America from direct attack;
(ii)	implementation of any undertakings made by Canada under the charter of the United Nations, or under the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, or other agreement for collective security;
(iii)	the organization to build up strength in a total war.
Supply-National Defence
Those objectives were absolutely definite. They were clearly stated. There was no ambiguity about them. Anyone could read them and be sure what was meant. This year there is a change in these defence objectives. To begin with, I should like to make it clear that I am not against change, and that I am not necessarily against this particular change. However, I should like to know what the explanation is and what the change in this year's objectives really means. I will read this year's objectives from this year's white paper. They appear at page 3 thereof. You will note the difference, Mr. Chairman. The objectives are stated to be as follows:
Canada's defence program continues to be planned for the immediate defence of Canada-
That was the same as last year, but now we begin to get into the differences:
-for co-operation with the United States in the joint defence of the Canada-United States region, for co-operation within the North Atlantic Treaty Organization looking towards the provision of a collective force capable of deterring aggression, and for carrying out undertakings by Canada as a member of the United Nations Organization.
Instead of having objectives numbered 1, 2 and 3, absolutely clear and simple, we have one long sentence this year in which the objectives are not set out very definitely and in which they are merged into one another.
I should like to consider just what some of these changes are in detail and ask the minister about them. When he comes to reply he can perhaps answer the questions. I should like to ask what these changes mean and why they are there. Why is it that, instead of having as the first objective, as we have had for several years previously, "the immediate defence of Canada and North America from direct attack", we now have "the immediate defence of Canada"-that is the same-and then "for co-operation with the United States in the joint defence of the Canada-United States region"?
We all realize that co-operation with the United States in the defence of North America is essential. We cannot defend the continent by ourselves. We cannot defend our own country from air attack by ourselves. We must do it in alliance and in co-operation with the United States. We all agree with that. However, does the change in these objectives and stating them in these terms indicate, shall we say, a quiet way of introducing into our defence objectives and defence policy the idea that we are to be more dependent on the United States? Is that the implication or the meaning of that change?
As was stated by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich this morning, we already have in this country some 3,000 United States troops and, judging by what we have been
4908	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence told, we are to have many thousands more to man this distant early warning line which is now under construction. As 1 say, is this change in our defence objectives or in the way they are stated an indication of increasing dependence on the United States and on their defence plans and so on? Is it, shall we say, a first indication of an over-all command which Air Marshal Slemon in his speech not long ago indicated was a necessity as far as North America's air defence was concerned?
Perhaps most Canadians are not going to be too much opposed to these things if that is the case, but I think it is up to the Minister of National Defence to tell us. I do not think we should be left in doubt as to what is the situation, or as to what are the plans in that regard at the present time.
The next phase in these objectives for this year is this:
-for co-operation within the North Atlantic Treaty Organization looking towards the provision of a collective force capable of deterring aggression,-
Previously this objective was not "cooperation within NATO" but it was "implementation of any undertakings made by Canada . . . under the North Atlantic Treaty Organization". Does this change indicate our commitments under NATO have now changed? Does it indicate that rather than having commitments under NATO which it is one of our defence objectives to implement, it has now become a matter of no commitments but that we are merely going to cooperate with NATO in regard to our joint defence? That change in wording may mean nothing or it may mean a good deal. I think the minister should tell us what it means, particularly as there is no such change as far as the United Nations is concerned, because our present objectives go on to read in this way:
-and for carrying out undertakings by Canada as a member of the United Nations Organization.
In other words, one of our objectives is still to carry out undertakings under the United Nations; but whereas the objective used to be "the implementation of undertakings under NATO", it has been changed to "co-operation within NATO". It seems as though a distinction has been made between our position under NATO and our position under the United Nations, which was not there previously. It was "implementation of" in both cases previously.
We now come to what was the third of our objectives previously, namely "the organization to build up strength in a total war". What has happened to that objective?
It has disappeared altogether. I do not think the minister would say that objective has


been reached. I do not think he would say that we have built up all the organization required to meet the demands of a total war. I therefore wonder why that has been dropped as one of our objectives. As a matter of fact, I would say you never really reach that objective. It is one you keep working toward constantly, but you never actually reach it.
It seems a little peculiar that this objective, which has been there for the last four or five years, has now suddenly been dropped and does not appear any more.

It has been in for the past four years. It is just the same as complete air defence of the country. You can never achieve complete air defence of the country. On the basis of your argument we should not have a plane, we should not man a radar station, we should not have any defence at all. I think that interjection is an indication of the type of thinking of some people with respect to defence matters, and it is extremely shallow. I should like to ask the minister particularly about the dropping of this third objective, the organization to build up strength in the event of a total war. Does this mean less interest in the reserves?
I am going to come back to the reserves later and have something more to say about them, but in the white paper and the minister's speech I noted that not very much was said about the reserves. After all, the reserves are one of the big factors in what has been called the organization to build up strength in the event of a total war. They are one of the big factors in that field in all three services, navy, army and air force. I hope this does not mean the reserves are going to be sort of gently pushed aside and there is going to be far less interest taken in them. We have reason to fear that from the fact that so little has been said about them in the white paper and by the minister in this debate.
In the white paper the emphasis has been placed on the danger of thermonuclear attack. Every member who has taken part in the debate has referred to that. Every speaker has stressed it, and I think properly so. I should like to read part of what is said in connection with this matter. On page 4 of the white paper there is the following:
For North America the possibility appears for the first time of an attack that could cripple the military and industrial potential of Canada and the United States. Should we ever be attacked with thermonuclear weapons, it is plain that our immediate problem would be national survival

I agree with the latter part of that statement only too fully. However, I must point out that the government has been extremely slow in coming to a realization of the danger facing us. This is the first white paper in which any real cognizance has been taken of the danger of atomic and thermonuclear attack. As far as thermonuclear attack is concerned, the possibility has been there for upwards of two years. As far as atomic attack is concerned it has been there for considerably longer. This is not a new thing at all. For several years past it has been quite possible for us to be attacked with atomic weapons. The government should have realized this fact long ago, and attempts should have been made to meet the situation long before now. It is only this year that any real attempt is being made to meet the extremely great danger.
It is quite true that an atomic attack would not have been as bad as an attack by hydrogen bombs. However, it still would have more or less crippled our military and industrial potential, inflicting damage which would have required quite a long time to repair. It is quite true that the hydrogen bomb is much more destructive. It is true that the Russians have jet bombers that are faster and capable of flying greater distances than they had two, three or four years ago, but it is really a matter of degree more than anything else. The basic danger is greater but it existed before and, as I say, I think the government is culpable in that it did not take the necessary steps earlier to meet the danger.
The belated recognition of the danger of this country's entire life being crippled by atomic and thermonuclear weapons has apparently led now to a realization of the necessity for a change in defence policy. It is quite apparent from what the minister has said that the government believes greater emphasis must be placed on the air arm, and especially on radar warning screens and fighter aircraft to back up the screens. I should like to point out to him that a great deal of the discussion last year was on these very points. We pointed out that the existing radar screen, the "Pinetree" line, really constituted only point defence and was far too close to targets to be of any real good. We also pointed out that our fighter defences to back up the warning screen were almost negligible, and that what was required was an extension of the screens and a very considerable increase in our fighter strength.
As a matter of fact, some of us suggested last year that until the fighter strength in this country could be built up, some of the fighter squadrons then in Europe should be 50433-310
Supply-National Defence brought back here to look after the defence of Canada. In my opinion that is something that should still be given serious consideration, because it is going to be a considerable length of time before our fighter strength is built up sufficiently to give us even a semi-defence, may I say.
As the minister said several times this morning, complete defence is impossible. Everybody recognizes that, but we certainly should have the best defence against atomic and thermonuclear attack that the economy of the country can provide and that our whole defence activities can make possible. The unfortunate fact is we have not got it. In fact we have, and have had right along, lamentably little.
Last year and in previous years the former defence minister always attempted to lull the country into a false sense of security by assuring us that everything was pretty well all right and we did not need to worry. I am sorry to say that a certain attempt along the same line still seems to be apparent. I had hoped the present minister would not fall into the same great error of trying to lull the house and the country into a false sense of security, but from some of the statements in the white paper it would appear that the temptation was a bit too much for him. For example, on page 5 we find the following:
Nine regular squadrons and ten auxiliary squadrons of the Royal Canadian Air Force are maintained in Canada to provide fighter aircraft for interception duties. By the end of 1955 all nine regular squadrons will be completely equipped with long-range, all-weather CF-100 jet aircraft.
I think that gives the casual reader a totally wrong impression. We of course have not nine squadrons now. I hope the minister is right in saying that by the end of this year these nine squadrons will be completely equipped with CF-100 jet aircraft, but if so it will be a different story from what was the case with the promises we received with respect to naval vessels, referred to this morning by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, which we were promised first in 1951 and have not received yet.
Unfortunately that has been the case with respect to many of the promises contained in white papers and ministerial statements on defence. The promises were not lived up to. Things came along later than we were led to expect they would. The real difficulty involved in the statement I have read is the fact that the ten auxiliary squadrons are not effective squadrons, and of course the minister knows that quite well. They really should not be counted as part of the fighter defence of Canada at the present time. The aircraft they have are obsolete. The number
4910	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence of aircraft they have is limited. In many cases their establishments are below strength, and so on. In other words, they are not effective fighter units which could go up and meet jet bombers.
The minister recognized this in the statement he made this morning, when he said that the position of these auxiliary fighter squadrons was being reconsidered, and the question of supplying them with the CF-100, about which we were told last year and the year before, was being reconsidered. Perhaps it was not feasible for these squadrons to handle the CF-100.
I should like to strongly reinforce what was said by the hon. member for Equimalt-Saanich and by the leader of this party, that if these ten auxiliary squadrons are not to be supplied with the CF-lOO's, if they are not to be supplied with sufficient regular air force personnel to make it feasible and possible for them to operate as CF-100 squadrons, then there is a strong necessity to have them replaced by or converted into regular air force squadrons.
What the minister said this morning, and the way the white paper reads, is a sufficient tacit admission that nine fighter squadrons are not sufficient to back up the radar screens and defend some of the likely targets, such as the big cities and industrial areas of this country. Since this reconsideration is taking place, I would hope it might result in something definite that would provide us with at least ten additional effective squadrons.
Now,. Mr. Chairman, the question arises, what is the present defence policy? We have not been told either in the white paper or in what the minister has said. We have heard and read a great many words, but we have not been definitely told what the defence policy is. The white paper contains a very apparent truism on page 3 in connection with policy:
A central problem in all current military planning is the nature of the balance to be maintained between conventional forces and weapons and those for atomic and nuclear warfare.
I think we could all agree with that. It is certainly a very critical problem. How does the government propose to solve it? We have not been told, and I think perhaps that is the crux of the whole defence policy. We are still in complete ignorance on that very important point. We know, of course, that changes in emphasis are necessary. The minister has said that, and we have been saying it for years. There is nothing new in that. The big question is, what are these changes? What is the general concept to be. I think the minister should suggest that, but he has not done so thus far.


I think there is no doubt that great differences of opinion have existed on the part of the senior officers of the three services, and they have been in the process of being threshed out lately. It would be extremely peculiar if there were not these great differences of opinion. The speech I referred to earlier, made by Air Marshal Slemon, and the speech made by Air Vice Marshal Plant, I believe are indicative of the arguments that have been taking place and the differences of opinion with regard to policy which must necessarily exist in a time of change such as this. It would seem to me that the retirement of General Simonds and the other personnel changes which have taken place recently are probably indicative of the same thing. What we would like to know is, have these differences been resolved? Has any clear, definite policy been decided upon? If so, what is it? That is what I should like to hear from the Minister of National Defence before this debate concludes, and particularly before the consideration of the estimates is finished.
It has been apparent for years that we needed greater air defence for Canada. The minister mentioned that. A considerable improvement along this line is apparently now under way through the provision of these radar screens and the increase in the number of fighter squadrons. As has been stated, our first defence responsibility is to prevent, so far as possible, air attack on our cities with thermonuclear and atomic weapons. Everybody agrees with that. We agree that the only practical means are the radar lines and the fighters, and, we hope, ground-to-air guided missiles.
The minister spoke briefly about those, and I thought somewhat discouragingly. From what I had read of the experience in the United States and Great Britain these ground-to-air guided missiles had been reasonably satisfactory. A considerable number have already been installed, particularly in the United States. It would seem to me that unless there is some serious difficulty in connection with them, about which we have not heard, we should be getting some of them around our most important targets in Canada.
Connected with this prime danger which faces the country, of course, and the prime responsibility of defence, is that of warning the population of this country of any impending air attack, to have a civil defence organization and plans for the evacuation of our large cities. Of course there should be plans for handling and feeding of the population of these cities once they are evacuated. I was very glad to see the emphasis that was placed on civil defence

in this white paper. I hope that much more of a concrete nature will be done so far as civil defence measures are concerned than has been the case in Canada up to date. We have chiefly talked about civil defence and done very little about it in a concrete way. The dominion government has refused to face the situation, and has refused to meet its responsibilities along that line.
When civil defence was moved from the Department of National Defence to that of health and welfare a few years ago, many of us hoped it might result in a considerable improvement in civil defence measures. This hope has been to a large extent unrealized. As is stated in this white paper, the present threat is the complete crippling of the military and industrial potential of this nation. It would appear to me that possibly a serious mistake was made in moving civil defence from the Department of National Defence to health and welfare. It seems to me now that civil defence is an integral part of defence, and there is just a difference between military defence and civil defence. The two are tied so closely together that military personnel are perhaps going to have to take a large part in what is called civil defence. Probably we should move the civil defence section back under the defence department, and have all our defence activities thoroughly integrated.
After providing for the prime need of defence against air attack-and this, of course, in close co-operation with the United States, which is essential-we might ask, what else is required in our defence? Many people, including Mr. Churchill, who is a most eminent authority, have stated that they believe an atomic stalemate may have been reached.
I hope that is correct, and I think there is a fair amount of reason for that hope, that we have reached a situation where both sides have a large atomic and thermonuclear stockpile, the use of which, so far as each side is concerned, would be so totally destructive that neither would use it.
The hon. member for Okanagan Boundary who spoke for the C.C.F. quoted Mr. Hanson Baldwin and others, including General Montgomery, to the effect that in the event of war it was definite that atomic weapons would be used. He said we must take it for granted that this is so. I would point out, however, that those statements were made some time ago; they were not made within the last few months. I would be much more inclined to accept the appreciation of the situation by Sir Winston Churchill, who says there is a good chance of reaching at least an atomic stalemate, and that as a result we will never have the wholesale 50433-310}
Supply-National Defence destruction of the world which would follow an atomic or hydrogen bomb attack by one side against the other.
Nevertheless that is a prime danger. That is the thing we must guard against; and I do not for one moment suggest that we should relax our defence efforts in the slightest degree. That is the thing, above all others, which we must guard against and must be prepared to meet. However, if Sir Winston Churchill's appreciation of the situation is correct, what it means is that future wars may be small wars, such as we had in Korea. Or it might amount to a third large world war, but fought with conventional weapons, fought to a great extent with armies, navies and air forces using older types of bombs and the like.
It seems to me quite apparent that so long as that possibility exists to any great extent, this country must continue to be equipped with an army and a navy along somewhat conventional lines. No country has done away with its army and navy. We have seen no evidence of the push-button warfare which some people have been talking about. I take it that our commitments to the United Nations and to NATO require us to have a certain number of these conventional forces.
As the leader of this party said this afternoon, what we need is conventional forces used unconventionally. It seems to me that what has been said by other members in this party is correct when they point out that the organization of our conventional forces is out of date and should be brought up to date. We must improve their mobility and their hitting power.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has spoken this year and in other years about a greater use of armour. Tests which have been made with atomic weapons indicate that armoured vehicles give a very high degree of protection. If we are going to have atomic warfare, probably the only troops who will survive anywhere near the point where the atomic bomb is dropped will be those protected by armour. The hon. member has pointed out that the use of such armour would have the effect of saving the lives of troops using conventional weapons such as machine guns and rifles.
It seems to me quite apparent that in our present armed forces we place far too great dependence on straight infantry of the old style. It is true that we have one airborne brigade; but the rest of the army, including the division and the other brigade, are the conventional 1939-45 style of infantry | to a large extent armed with the same or
4912	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence similar weapons. There have been some changes, of course, but the weapons are very much the same. This is out of date and should be changed so we would have mobile forces, which would be better protected and would hit harder.
Let me say something with regard to the manpower question. The maximum strength of our forces has been set at 120,000 and that strength has been almost reached, with an enlistment of 117,000. It is evident from the white paper and from what the minister has said that the air arm is going to need more men. It will not be able to man these additional squadrons and the increased number of radar stations without a considerable increase in the number of men. From what the minister said I take it there is no idea of securing these men. He did not admit that more men would be needed, but that seems evident. He did not say they were going to be taken from the army and the navy, and that those services were going to be reduced in order to provide the increased number required by the air force, but I am wondering if that is not so. I wonder if that is not the point to which we are moving.
I suggest it is quite evident that with this
120,000	men we have not enough manpower because, to begin with, we have several thousand Americans in Canada at the present time, and many thousands more are coming when the D.E.W. line is built. There is no question that the Americans will get the greatest benefit from these radar lines because they are farther away from the possible enemy than we are. Therefore they will have a longer period of warning than we would have. It is clear therefore that their proportionate benefit is greater than ours, because they will receive a longer period of warning. And of course these warning lines are just as essential to them as they are to us, in fact even more so.
I think everyone would agree they should pay the major portion of the cost of those lines, and apparently they are going to do so. As I understand it, they are going to construct this D.E.W. line pretty much at their own expense, and will man it. They have also paid a good proportion of the cost of the "Pinetree" line.
I believe there will be no argument as to the equity of that arrangement. They are getting great benefit from these lines and should pay a major portion of the cost. But I submit that is a totally different matter from having their troops man these lines. That would not be consistent with our sovereignty and our independence as a nation, unless it were a matter of absolute necessity. I understand one of these lines will not be
[Mr. Harkness.l

ready for a long time, and we could probably have men trained to man it. Once we have the trained personnel it seems to me we could man those lines ourselves. It is not consistent with our general national pretensions to do otherwise.
It seems to me peculiar and rather unreasonable that while the United States and most of the other NATO countries have a greater proportion of their manpower in the services than we have, at the same time we are asking one of these countries, namely the United States, to bring in men to man one of the radar lines in our country. I should like to ask a general question, Mr. Chairman. What relation do the 120,000 men in our forces actually bear to our real defence needs? It seems to me that is an arbitrary figure. I cannot see any real relation of that figure of
120.000	to our defence needs. It is a figure we have had now for some time. I should like an explanation from the minister as to how that figure is arrived at. Why not
110.000	or 150,000? It seems to be purely arbitrary, as I say, and it needs to be explained.
I should like to say something about our reserve forces. They continue, as was stated by the leader of our party this afternoon, to be one of the chief bases for the recruitment of the regular forces. People are attracted into the reserve. As they become interested, many of them go on to recruit into the regular forces. It is most important to carry on our reserve forces. They are the basis on which we must organize in the event of a total war. As was stated in all previous white papers, they are the basis upon which we must mobilize, and it does not seem to me that nearly enough attention is being paid to them.
As I indicated earlier, I am afraid the general idea is getting around: oh, well, the reserve forces are all right, but still we have the regular forces and therefore we do not need to worry too much about the reserves. If they gradually wither away it is too bad, but it is not too important.
I would be afraid, even from what the minister said about reassessing, that these ten auxiliary squadrons are going to do that. Perhaps they have in mind just to let these auxiliary squadrons run downhill, shall we say, or disintegrate. Therefore I should like the minister to make a more definite statement than has been made in regard to policy so far as the defence forces are concerned.
I think the defence forces are very necessary from another point of view. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich indicated that they could be tied in with civil defence. It is essential that they should be tied in with civil

defence, but there is another feature of civil defence particularly. Perhaps it should not really be called civil defence, as it is. If we had an atomic bombing attack on this country one of the greatest dangers, as far as survivors are concerned, would be the matter of panic, chaos and so forth. It would give an opportunity for enemy agents, saboteurs, fifth columnists, and so forth, to go ahead and destroy what was left, and it would also provide opportunity for the criminal fringe of the population, which is normally held in check by the police force, to indulge in what would be their normal activities if we did not have the usual police and security forces to stop them.
Therefore under these circumstances a very considerable security force would be needed, and that is a job which the reserve forces, if they were in good shape, if they were in any sort of reasonable numbers, would be admirably equipped to do. It is a job which would be necessary if complete chaos were not to continue for perhaps quite a long time in the terrible event of an atomic attack. Therefore, from that point of view alone, the providing of security forces which would be scattered throughout the whole country, the reserve forces should be maintained, should be brought up to strength as far as possible, should be encouraged in every way.

At the outset, before trying to answer at least some of the questions and points which have been raised, I should like to thank hon. members on the other side of the house for the helpful remarks they have made today, for the way they have approached this debate and the keen interest they have shown, which of course one would expect, in our national defence effort. It has been a first-class debate. I think I have learned some things; I hope we all have.
If I might, without making an invidious comparison, I should like particularly to compliment the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich on the excellemt speech which he made this morning. There is not too much I can disagree with in his speech, but there are a couple of points I might possibly refer to. One had to do with a remark he made, if I took him down correctly. He intimated that the only place in which the war could be lost was on the sea and air approaches to this continent. He was developing, I think, the importance of continental defence. He developed it in this way. He said our entire
Supply-National Defence defence effort should be designed from now on with one point in mind, namely the defence of the approaches to this continent. He may not have intended to emphasize that phase of it so much, but I should like to remind him and the committee that this of course minimizes, if not ignores, the concept of NATO.
Our position would be very difficult if, with our immediate sea and air approaches guarded strongly, we were confronted with a western Europe in enemy hands. It is a vision that we would not like to contemplate. While it is true that the last battle in any future war would certainly be fought for the control of this continent, I think we cannot for a moment in our defence effort consider leaving western Europe inadequately defended, because we all know that we are one organization, and the protection of each is of course for the benefit of us all.
There was one other point which was also mentioned by the hon. member for Calgary North with respect to the first Canadian division. He referred to the nature of its composition and training as not being suitable for the defence of this country. I should like to point out to hon. members that the first Canadian division is, of course, a division under NATO primarily for the defence of Europe. Our own mobile striking force is the primary force for any diversionary attacks on this country. It is highly trained, well-equipped and airborne. It is a strong hitting force that we would utilize in this country.
The Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich and the hon. member for Calgary North made very proper inquiries as to whether or not the internal organization, the functional set-up of the army, is such as to be in touch with modern developments and to meet new situations. I might say that considerable studies are going on here and, also, there is a good deal of cooperation with military authorities in the United States and in the United Kingdom who are making intensive studies of the set-up of army units and army formations in the light of modern conditions and the new types of warfare. This summer at Gagetown our own troops will be trying out new dispositions and new tactics in the light of our present knowledge of the use of atomic weapons.
The changes that are taking place and that will take place are bound to be of a gradual nature. I think I can say that we are keeping reasonably well abreast of developments as they are being worked out in other countries and as new conditions make it necessary for our services to meet them.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary, the hon. member for Wetaskiwin, the hon.

Supply-National Defence member for Calgary North and possibly some others referred to the utilization of the forces, particularly the militia, in connection with civil defence operations. We are in fact co-operating to an increasing degree. The G.O.C.'s of all our army commands have formulated plans for each of their units to render assistance should need arise. Arrangements have also been made for personnel from the civil defence college at Arnprior to visit the militia units and conduct courses in civil defence for militia officers.
The army, and indeed all the services, are stressing the need of being in a position to render whatever assistance we can, without of course intruding on the primary functions of the services. I think the experience following "Hurricane Hazel" and the other major disasters show a disposition on the part of the services to be most co-operative.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, the hon. member for Trinity-Conception and, I think, the hon. member for Wetaskiwin expressed some worry about the role of the navy; as to whether it was to be simply a convoy navy in the narrow sense of the phrase. I should like to tell the hon. members that while convoy duty is one of the navy's important functions, it is also trained and organized for the hunting and killing of submarines apart from convoy duty.
I think it was the hon. member for Oxford who referred to helicopters, and I might tell him that we have an experimental squadron of helicopters in the Royal Canadian Navy which is developing suitable tactics for submarine hunting.
