I have it here that the hon. member asked if we had it. The hon. member for Oxford and also the hon. member for Trinity-Conception asked for additional information with regard to the mine-sweeping activities of the navy. I might tell them that there is a mine-sweeping squadron on the Pacific and on the Atlantic coast whose duties are tied in closely with harbour defence activities, protecting the main ports on each coast.
The hon. member for Okanagan Boundary seemed to have the idea that all our equipment was obsolete or obsolescent. On listening to him I gathered that he had obtained his information from a variety of sources, and there seemed to be some confusion as to the weapons he was discussing. At one point he mentioned a weapon which I happen to know will not be coming into use until 1960. He mentioned also as being obsolete, among other things, the 3-inch 50 calibre


naval gun which is now actually in production simultaneously both for the Royal Canadian Navy and the United States navy. In the view of the United States navy this gun is certainly not obsolete.
While I would not say that all our weapons are the very latest, any more than those of any other country, still I do not think the obsolescence factor which the hon. member alleged is anything like as prominent as he sought to make it. I am afraid also that
I	cannot agree with the hon. member that the chances of war have been reduced almost to the vanishing point. I think the danger of war is still very great, and this is a pertinent factor in our thinking. It is only as long as we are able to continue to lead from strength, and with all our fellow nations in the free world working with us, that we can hope ultimately to remove that danger.
I should like to say to the hon. member for Oxford and the hon. member for Wetaskiwin that we have no intention of establishing a submarine arm in the Royal Canadian Navy. We have, however, made arrangements for training with submarines for personnel of the Royal Canadian Navy. I think it was the hon. member for Oxford who wondered whether the submarines we were getting from Great Britain were old and antiquated. I understand that those now serving with the Canadian navy were built since world war
II	and are considered to be modern and up to date.
The hon. member for York-Scarborough is to be commended on his interest in electronics research. I have noted with interest the suggestions he made. I think his suggestions are rather ambitious, but I do appreciate his interest in the subject.
The hon. member for York West made many helpful comments with regard to the air force. I think I should read his speech in order to follow his formula for cost figures in producing aeroplanes under different conditions. I shall be glad to study his plan. I must admit that I perked up my ears when I heard him say, or at least thought I heard him say, that the alternative method would save about $100,000 a plane. If I find that I did hear him correctly I shall certainly pass that on to the Minister of Defence Production.
The hon. member for Oxford raised the question whether the figure of 20,000 officers and men for the Royal Canadian Navy took into account the personnel requirements for the 14 destroyer escorts. The answer is yes.
I always listen with interest when the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre produces his favourite military child. He always puts

forward his case with great feeling and persuasiveness and I think he has almost persuaded me to look at it closely again.

I think the changes are merely changes of phraseology made in the hope of approximating a situation which has changed somewhat. He referred to the fact that the build-up for total war had not been mentioned, but I should suppose that by now would be understood. After all, the whole objective of our defence effort is to build up strength, not necessarily strength that we along with our NATO allies will use, but nevertheless sufficient joint strength to make it unnecessary to use.
There are a number of other points which I have noted here but on which I have not specific information.
However, perhaps I could keep a note of these matters and deal with them on the detailed estimates. Most of them are smaller points. I could do that if it would be satisfactory to hon. members.
